leads.title: Show HN: ApiClay – Turn a Website, Google Sheet or Database into a Paid API
leads.description: Hi HN, I’m a reverse engineer, and I’ve seen the same problem repeatedly: people need data, but the path from “I need this” to “my app, agent, or workflow can use it” is messy. Vibe coders want a working endpoint in minutes. Developers want clean docs, predictable JSON, and no surprise integration work. Businesses want to enrich lists, monitor changes, and safely expose internal data. AI agents need APIs they can discover and call reliably. Sometimes, the API simply doesn't exist. ApiClay makes that whole loop easier. You can search a catalogue of APIs and datasets, inspect them in a playground, and copy ready-to-run JavaScript, Python, or cURL snippets into your app. Each API has its own reference, pricing, trials, and usage terms, so you can see what you’re calling before you go live. But ApiClay is not just an API marketplace. If the API you need does not exist, you can create one with Website to API: give it a page, map the fields you care about, and publish a stable JSON endpoint. It works with static and JavaScript-heavy pages, and can return clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links. You can also turn what you already have into an API: * MySQL, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Google Sheets, Airtable, Excel/CSV, and HTTP services can become API endpoints. * Import an OpenAPI/Swagger file to get docs, a playground, and billing for an existing API. * Publish only the fields you choose, control access, set trials, plans, usage limits, and pricing. * Aggregate multiple providers into one tidy response for comparison-style products. For AI, ApiClay exposes an MCP endpoint so Claude, ChatGPT, or custom agents can search for an API, inspect it, and call it. The idea is simple: instead of an agent hallucinating a data source, it finds a real API and returns an answer backed by live data. There are also practical data tools beyond discovery: * Websets / enrichment: upload a list, enrich each row, set a spend cap, and export the result. * Monitors: watch an API or webpage and receive a signed webhook when something changes. * Cloud browser: automate a browser session for pages behind clicks or JavaScript rendering, then return the values your app needs. * Extraction: turn a page into clean Markdown, JSON, text, or links without maintaining your own scraper. For people publishing APIs, credentials stay encrypted on ApiClay and are not exposed to buyers; publishers control pricing, limits, trials, and access. For consumers, browsing and reading docs are free, while paid calls are charged per request and shown before use. *ApiClay is where you find the data API you need, build the one that is missing, let AI agents use it, and optionally sell it.* We’d love feedback from HN—especially from developers building data-heavy products, teams dealing with messy internal sources, and anyone experimenting with agent-driven workflows.

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: chunk(arr, 0) infinite-loops in .ltl stdlib; Python API raises raw ValueError
leads.description:
### Lateralus version

lateralus-lang 3.2.0

### Python version

Python 3.13.7

### Operating System

Linux

### Component

Standard Library

### Bug description

algorithms.chunk(arr, 0) has no size validation. In the .ltl stdlib version it
hangs forever (while-loop never advances because i = i + size with size == 0),
which freezes the VM with no error and no way to Ctrl+C from inside generated
code. In the Python API it raises a raw `ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be
zero`, which is an implementation detail leaking to the user.

Expected: a clear, early Value error for size <= 0 in both implementations.

### Reproduction code

```lateralus
import algorithms

fn main() {
    print("before")
    print(chunk([1, 2, 3], 0))   // hangs forever (never reaches "after")
    print("after")
}
```

### Expected behavior

Error before any work: chunk size must be a positive integer
(the program should exit non-zero, not hang)

### Actual behavior

```shell
# .ltl stdlib path — hangs forever (no error, CPU 100%, Ctrl+C needed)
$ lateralus run chunk_zero.ltl
before
^C

# Python API path:
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import chunk; chunk([1,2,3], 0)"
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File ".../lateralus_lang/algorithms.py", line 129, in chunk
    return [lst[i:i+n] for i in range(0, len(lst), n)]
ValueError: range() arg 3 must not be zero
```

### Additional context

Root cause (.ltl stdlib/algorithms.ltl):
    while i < len(arr) {
        let end = min(i + size, len(arr))
        result = result + [slice(arr, i, end)]
        i = i + size          # size == 0 → i never advances → infinite loop
    }
Suggested fix: guard size <= 0 (raise or return []) before the loop.

Python port (lateralus_lang/algorithms.py):
    def chunk(arr, size):
        return [arr[i:i + size] for i in range(0, len(arr), size)]
Suggested fix:
    if size <= 0:
        raise ValueError("chunk size must be a positive integer")

Environment: lateralus-lang 3.2.0 (PyPI), Python 3.13.7, Linux x86_64.
Drafted with AI assistance and reviewed before posting.

leads.description:
### Lateralus version

lateralus-lang 3.2.0

### Python version

Python 3.13.7

### Operating System

Linux

### Component

Standard Library

### Bug description

Two edge-case bugs in the Python API of lateralus_lang.algorithms
(the .ltl stdlib version already guards n < 2, so this is a
Python-port-only correctness/isolation issue):

1) primes_up_to(0)  -> IndexError: list assignment index out of range
   primes_up_to(-5) -> [2, 3]  (bogus; negative ranges produce primes)

2) sliding_window([1,2,3], 0) -> [[], [], [], []]
   Silent semantic trap: no error, plausible-looking output.

### Reproduction code

```lateralus
// NOTE: this edge case is only reachable through the Python API
// (the .ltl stdlib primes_up_to already guards `n < 2`).
// Minimal Python reproducer is in "Actual behavior" below.
import algorithms

fn main() {
    print(primes_up_to(10))   // [2, 3, 5, 7] — correct
}
```

### Expected behavior

primes_up_to(0)             -> []
primes_up_to(-5)            -> []
sliding_window([1,2,3], 0)  -> Value error (or [])

### Actual behavior

```shell
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import primes_up_to, sliding_window"
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import primes_up_to; primes_up_to(0)"
IndexError: list assignment index out of range
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import primes_up_to; print(primes_up_to(-5))"
[2, 3]
$ python3 -c "from lateralus_lang.algorithms import sliding_window; print(sliding_window([1,2,3], 0))"
[[], [], [], []]
```

### Additional context

Suggested fix:
    def primes_up_to(n: int) -> list:
        if n < 2:
            return []
        ...
    def sliding_window(arr: list, size: int) -> list:
        if size <= 0:
            raise ValueError("window size must be a positive integer")
        ...

leads.title: [bounty]: bug-report: Python optional pipeline silently converts valid falsy results to nil
leads.description:
### Lateralus version

3.2.0 (from pyproject.toml and lateralus_lang.__version__; tested commit d078809df3f5db544b7efa7b0979c7a43ebb25e6)

### Python version

Python 3.11.9

### Operating System

Windows

### Component

Compiler / Parser

### Bug description

The Python backend incorrectly converts valid falsy return values into `None` (`nil`) when using the optional pipeline operator `|?`.

When the input is not `nil`, the operator should call the function and preserve its return value. However, the generated Python code uses the `and ... or None` pattern, which incorrectly replaces falsy results such as `0`, `false`, `""`, `[]`, and `0.0` with `None`.

**Minimal example:**

```text
import io
fn zero(x: int) -> int { return 0 }
let result = 5 |? zero
io.println(result)
```

**Expected result:** `0`

**Actual result:** `None`

**Generated Python code:**

```python
result = ((_opt_val := 5) is not None and zero(_opt_val) or None)
```

The issue affects both direct function references and function calls with additional arguments.

The bug was reproduced in 10 test cases, with 5 additional control tests passing.

**Affected file:** `lateralus_lang/codegen/python.py`, lines 1492–1502.

**Tested version:** Lateralus 3.2.0, commit `d078809df3f5db544b7efa7b0979c7a43ebb25e6`.

This is a correctness bug that can silently cause data loss in optional pipelines.

### Reproduction code

```lateralus
import io

fn zero(x: int) -> int {
    return 0
}

let result = 5 |? zero
io.println(result)
```

### Expected behavior

The optional pipeline operator `|?` should execute the function when the input is not `nil` and preserve its return value.

In this example, the function `zero(5)` returns `0`, so the expected output is:

```
0
```

Valid falsy values such as `0`, `false`, `""`, `[]`, and `0.0` must not be converted to `None`.

### Actual behavior

```shell
The program compiles successfully but prints `None` instead of `0`.

The Python backend generates:


result = ((_opt_val := 5) is not None and zero(_opt_val) or None)


Because `zero(_opt_val)` returns `0`, the Python `or None` expression incorrectly replaces the valid result with `None`.

This causes silent loss of valid falsy values.
```

### Additional context

**Additional testing evidence:**

- Tested on Lateralus 3.2.0 (Python backend).
- 15 regression tests executed in an isolated Windows AppContainer.
- 10 test cases reproduced the bug.
- 5 control tests passed.
- No matching duplicate was found among the inspected public issues, pull requests, and comments at the time of testing.

**Bounty eligibility:**

I would like to submit this report for the recurring $10 bug-report micro-bounty described in BOUNTIES.md.

The investigation was completed before opening a reservation issue. I understand this differs from the project's pre-claim procedure.

Could the maintainer please confirm whether this report is still eligible for the bounty?

I can provide the full regression results and additional reproduction

leads.title: Show HN: Formstep, Request information from customers without the back-and-forth
leads.description: I built Formstep: https://formstep.io The idea came from a problem I kept running into while working on loan applications. A workflow could automate a large part of the process, but eventually it would need something only the customer could provide: a document, a correction, a signature, an explanation, or confirmation of some information. At that point, workflow automation basically did not work. The forms themselves were also often the source of the problem. Applications came in with wrong documents, misunderstood questions, incomplete answers, or people simply forgetting to finish. Someone had to email the customer, explain what was missing, wait for a reply then follow up again. It was always back-and-forth. So I built Formstep to make requesting information from customers easier, not only for humans, but also for workflows and AI agents. The idea is: A person, workflow, or AI agent sends a customer a request through email or a link. Either re-use existing form or create unique for each customer. You can prefill what you already know, lock fields, pass context, and only ask the customer what you need. For example, we might already know: * Address that you already have in the CRM * Company description from the internet * What a agreement document must contain * How a good answer should be Formstep can check inputs and uploaded files while the customer is filling out the form and tell them if something is missing or inconsistent before they submit. For example “The PDF does not contain your signature” or “Invoice total does not match the order amount”. The goal is to catch problems while the customer is still there, rather than letting bad data continue through the workflow and discovering it later. On the automation side, requests can currently be created through n8n, Zapier, the REST API, or by an AI agent over MCP. When the customer finishes, the structured answers can go back into the workflow so it can continue. Forms and invitation/reminder are multilingual, and submitted answers can be translated inside the dashboard with one click. If you want, Formstep can be used as normal form builder and shared through public links, QR, embeds etc. It support custom themes for dark/light mode, with cover image, has Notion-style editor and much more. The list is too long to fit here. I want to make Formstep a plattform where it becomes more intelligent over time and ensures that we can get better answers from customers for any use case. My question to you: Where do your automations currently stop because they need input from a customer or user, and how are you handling that today? If you are interested in trying out the n8n node: https://www.npmjs.com/package/n8n-nodes-formstep Zapier integration: https://zapier.com/apps/formstep/integrations Connecting your AI agent: https://docs.formstep.io/developers/mcp-server/ Docs: https://docs.formstep.io I would love your feedback and please try a quick demo at https://app.formstep.io/try

leads.title: [50 JNZ] Coroutine Flow variants of the two WebSocket subscriptions
leads.description:
`JanzeerRpcWs` delivers subscription events through callbacks only: `subscribeNewBlocks(params) { block -> … }` and `subscribeAddressActivity(addresses) { event -> … }`, each returning a `Subscription`. Kotlin and Android code usually wants a `Flow`, and today everyone has to write the same `callbackFlow` wrapper.

**What to do:** in `client/src/main/kotlin/org/janzeer/sdk/rpc/`, add

- `fun JanzeerRpcWs.newBlocksFlow(params: NewBlocksParams = NewBlocksParams()): Flow<…>`
- `fun JanzeerRpcWs.addressActivityFlow(addresses: List<String>): Flow<…>`

with the same element types the callbacks receive. Each is a cold flow built with `callbackFlow`: collecting it subscribes, cancelling the collector calls `Subscription.unsubscribe()` in `awaitClose`, and it never closes the socket (the caller owns the `JanzeerRpcWs`). Events must not be dropped silently: use `trySendBlocking` or a documented buffer, and say which in the KDoc. A failed subscribe call must fail the flow with the SDK's exception, not hang.

`kotlinx-coroutines-core` is an `implementation` dependency of the client module today; `Flow` in a public signature needs it as `api`. Keep the existing callback methods unchanged, and keep the Java-friendly surface (the new functions can be Kotlin-only extension functions in a new file).

**Acceptance:** tests in `client/src/test/kotlin/…` using the `MockWebServer` WebSocket pattern already in `RpcTest.kt`: events arrive in order; cancelling the collector sends the unsubscribe call; a subscribe error fails the flow. `./gradlew build` green, then `./gradlew apiDump` and commit the changed `*.api` files. Add a short section to `docs/json-rpc-and-subscriptions.md`, a line in `CHANGELOG.md`, and show in the pull request the output of collecting three blocks from `wss://explorer.janzeer.org/rpc/ws`.

No AI attribution trailers in commits, please.

leads.title: Show HN: Local Graph for Your Agents
leads.description: We all use different agentic systems, bots, chats, and so on. One day I realized that I need to copy context between the apps. It is annoying. So I created a trivial local MCP which sits on top of SQLite and exposes Cypher so LLM can query anything. Also LLM can define a schema if it understands it needs new nodes or edges. How do I use it: 1. I've scanned all my documents and stored passports, driver licences and all kind of contracts for my apartment, insurance and so on. And not only mine - the entire family. 2. I've extracted all the key date and values. Also gemini extracted all the personal relations. Like "Alex is-a-child-of Bob". "Bob is-married-to Anna". So i can ask "give me a passport number of my son" and it gives it back instantly. It might not be a big deal, but it is very convenient. 3. It stores all the projects I'm working on, key steps and decisions. 4. And the most important thing - it works from anywhere. I can ask Hermes i telegram to remind me when my insurance ends or I can reference my project in ClaudeCode just by name and it will get the entire history from Antigravity. I would be happy if you guys find it useful.

leads.title: [$50 BOUNTY] [Python] Add cross-platform health check fallbacks
leads.description:
**Bounty:** $50 (LT)

**Area:** `tools/health_check.py`

**Current state:** The health check tool reads Linux-only `/proc/meminfo` and `/proc/loadavg` directly for memory and load checks. On macOS or other non-Linux environments those checks degrade to warning-only results even though Python standard-library fallbacks can still provide useful diagnostics.

**What's needed:** Add cross-platform fallbacks for the memory and load checks so non-Linux environments report useful values instead of generic `/proc` read failures. Keep the Linux behavior compatible with the current output.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- `check_memory_usage()` keeps the existing `/proc/meminfo` path on Linux but has a non-Linux fallback that returns a meaningful status/detail tuple.
- `check_load_average()` keeps the existing `/proc/loadavg` path where available but falls back to `os.getloadavg()` or another standard-library path where possible.
- Add focused tests or a small validation path that simulates missing `/proc` files and verifies fallback behavior.
- JSON and text health-check output remain backward compatible for existing callers.
- PR description explains the fallback behavior and validation performed.

**Required validation:**
- Run `python3 build.py`
- Include the generated diagnostic `.logd` artifact from `diagnostic/build-XXX.logd` in the PR; also include `diagnostic/build-XXX.json` if present
- Use `.github/pull_request_template.md` for your submission

leads.title: Show HN: Revix AI – PR review against the standards your repo follows
leads.description: Hello, I’m Oscar. I’ve been leading dev teams from Barcelona with my cofounder Uri for a long time. We pushed the use of AI a lot, allowing an increase in the code shipment velocity, but our job as seniors moved from building to just reviewing. We also started to see a lot of drift in how devs were doing the code, less standards, less control, which caused more bugs and differences between what product department asked and what we shipped. It was impossible for us to keep reviewing everything by hand, so we decided to clone how we review as humans into a product: Revix AI. In easy words, Revix main strength is that it extracts from your repo all the good practices and team standards, then on every pull request comments if anything moves from that. That, paired with PR status badges and targeted notifications allowed us to reduce review time by 54% on many teams, while increasing the confidence and reducing bugs on production. We know there are other similar products around and they work fine, but we found that they trust too much on the LLM and focus just on bug hunting. Our philosophy goes further, we created a system that reviews the same as a senior engineer would do, not catching just bugs. We achieved to comment only on things devs actually fix and stop the noise. Revix AI works on GitHub, Gitlab, Bitbucket and can sync with many other tools like Slack, Jira, Linear etc. Please feel free to request any other tool that we still do not support. We offer free reviews for any open source project, and for companies we do price per seat including a 14 days free trial. If you want to see Revix AI working, you can check this example PR: https://github.com/revix-app/fastapi-revix/pull/1 And here is one from an open source project that use many other reviewers so you can compare: https://github.com/ontogr/ontogr-agent-memory/pull/19 We want to work very closely with the community, so feel free to try it out and give us feedback, we love to keep improving and listen to all the customers and developers that try our tool.

leads.title: Launch HN: Simantic (YC F26) – Firmware Simulation for AI Agents
leads.description: Hi HN, we're Ahnaf and Seungmin from Simantic ( https://simantic.com ). We are building the simulation layer that lets engineers and AI agents test and validate firmware without hardware. Before Simantic, we were ex-firmware engineers at companies like Neuralink and Tesla. We’ve worked on some of the coolest projects, like the Cybertruck and Roadster, back when they were still early prototypes. We started working on firmware back when ChatGPT didn’t exist yet, but over the years, we saw how much of the engineering and development work has been automated as the frontier models improved to this point. In software, AI can run and test code inside your computer in a matter of seconds. But as firmware engineers, we didn’t have that luxury. An AI agent can write firmware in seconds, but in order to test it, we had to flash a physical board, then manually run tests using expensive and clunky tools with software made over a decade ago. To speed up the validation loop, we built the simulation layer that lets AI agents test the firmware and make decisions based on evidence, instead of waiting for the engineer to run tests for them. We used to spend hours testing our firmware manually on devboards, but now we use our own simulation to validate firmware in seconds. What we offer: - Virtual devboards you can program and run with a single API call, without leaving your terminal. - An AI code reviewer for firmware, that makes informed decisions based on evidence, using our simulation as a verification engine. - A CI/CD pipeline for your hardware projects that validates your firmware against a simulated version of the microcontroller on every commit. Here is a demo of our simulation used in an AI code review session: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kBK1ZjGWWbQ Our users are using Simantic for bare-metal and RTOS development for applications like flight controllers, electric vehicles, robotics, and satellites. For safety critical systems like avionics and automotives, a robust simulation system is incredibly important, because every change in the firmware puts a human life at stake, especially for machines that cost hundreds of thousands to millions of dollars. We recently helped an early stage space startup building satellites, to test their firmware on hardware that they don't yet have. Even the development modules for those satellites costs over $100k, and we helped them do that at just a hundredth of the cost and time. Early on in our journey, we established our idea to make better simulation but didn’t have a clear idea of how we would do it, we considered developing our software around open source emulation frameworks like Renode ( https://github.com/renode/renode ) and QEMU ( https://www.qemu.org/ ), because they were tools already used within the firmware industry. We built our MVP that was essentially a wrapper around Renode, but we quickly realized there were a lot of limitations to doing this. 1. We were bottlenecked by the development speed of Renode themselves. We tried making contributions on Github to fix issues we came across, but the speed in which we could merge our features in was not fast enough for a startup like us trying to move fast. 2. Yes, there were a breadth of features, but we had a lot of things we had to work around just because we couldn’t remove or change them. Users were complaining about simulation accuracy. leads.title: [20 JNZ] Example: accept a payment (watch an address, match the memo, confirm it is final)
leads.description:
The examples show how to send and how to watch, but not the thing a shop or a bot needs: "tell me when *this* payment has arrived". On Janzeer a block is final when it is committed, so the flow is short.

**What to do:** `examples/08_accept_payment.py`, about 40 lines, in the style of `examples/02_subscribe_address_activity.py` (asyncio, `JanzeerRpcWs` + `AsyncJanzeerClient`):

1. Make an invoice: a recipient address (`JANZEER_E2E_RECIPIENT`), an amount (`"0.5"`) and a random reference such as `inv-3f9a2c`.
2. `subscribe_address_activity([recipient], handler)`.
3. So that the example runs unattended, pay the invoice from the test wallet (`JANZEER_E2E_MNEMONIC`): `TxBuilder.transfer(sender=…, to=…, amount=…, nonce=…, data=<reference>, network_id=…)`.
4. In the handler, accept only the event whose `transaction` is a transfer to the recipient, whose `data` equals the reference and whose `amount` is at least the invoice amount. Compare amounts with `decimal.Decimal` or the SDK's amount helpers, never with `float`. Ignore every other event.
5. Confirm with `await_finality` that the status is `FINAL`, print `paid: inv-… 0.5 JNZ in block N`, unsubscribe and close.
6. Exit non-zero with a clear message if nothing matches within `EXAMPLE_SECONDS` (default 90).

Add it to the README's Examples paragraph and a line in `CHANGELOG.md`. The examples are run in a loop against the local test network (`CONTRIBUTING.md`), so it must finish on its own. `ruff check .` and `mypy` clean.

**Reference:** `docs/json-rpc-and-subscriptions.md`, `docs/asyncio.md`. No AI attribution trailers in commits, please.

The SDK is meant to be used from plain Java too, but the only Java example is the transfer quickstart (`examples/src/main/java/org/janzeer/examples/JavaQuickstart.java`). Subscriptions from Java need a detail that trips people: the callback is a Kotlin function type, so the lambda must return `Unit.INSTANCE`.

**What to do:** `examples/src/main/java/org/janzeer/examples/JavaWatchNewBlocks.java`, about 35 lines, the Java twin of `WatchNewBlocks.kt`:

- `JanzeerRpcWs.connect(url)` with `JANZEER_WS_URL` (default `ws://localhost:7019/rpc/ws`), in try-with-resources (`JanzeerRpcWs` is `Closeable`).
- Start two blocks below the tip (`ws.getTip()`), `ws.subscribeNewBlocks(new NewBlocksParams(fromHeight, false), block -> { …; return Unit.INSTANCE; })`.
- Print height, the first 12 characters of the hash, the producer and the transaction count for each block.
- Stop after `EXAMPLE_BLOCKS` blocks (default 3) or `EXAMPLE_SECONDS` (default 40), then `unsubscribe()` and close.

Run with `./gradlew :examples:run -PmainClass=org.janzeer.examples.JavaWatchNewBlocks`. Add it to the README's Examples paragraph, a sentence in `docs/java.md` next to the existing lambda note, and a line in `CHANGELOG.md`. It must work against the public node (`JANZEER_WS_URL=wss://explorer.janzeer.org/rpc/ws`); paste that output in the pull request. `./gradlew build` green (no public API change, so no `apiDump`).

### Objective & Acceptance Test
Evaluate eBPF syscall, process, and network policy enforcement plus structured audit streams for agent sandboxes. Run escape-attempt and policy-regression tests; measure syscall overhead and false positives.

### Scope & Canonical Architecture
Tracked in `hanzoai/cloud` with label `visor` (`hanzoai/visor` has issues disabled).

Canonical stack boundaries MUST stay intact (`vfs -> hanzoai/s3 -> visor`, Cloud owning lifecycle & billing, Enso routing models, Zen generating outputs, Kai returning structured non-generative decisions). Reported figures in referenced FAST/conference papers belong strictly to the original authors' environments and MUST NOT be treated as Hanzo expectations until reproduced here.

### Research-to-PR Acceptance Contract (0 of 6 requirements)
- [ ] **1. Paper & License Audit**: Link primary paper/code, summarize design, and verify license compatibility (prefer Apache-2.0/MIT for production merges; clean-room implementation or research-only report otherwise) and patent restrictions.
- [ ] **2. Matched Baselines**: Provide reproducible upstream baseline and identical Hanzo baseline scripts/configs.
- [ ] **3. Falsifiable Hypothesis**: Document target metrics and expected failure modes up front.
- [ ] **4. Deliverable**: Submit bounded implementation PR (Implementation Bounty) or documented reproducible experiment including valid negative results (Research Bounty).

leads.title: Show HN: TrnRT – An open-source LLM inference engine for AWS Trainium
leads.description: Hi HN, Sanchit here from RunAnywhere (YC W26). We just open-sourced TrnRT: Trainium RunTime, our inference engine for AWS Trainium. We started 3 weeks back, and currently we’re able to serve and run GLM 5.3 flash (FP8) on AWS trn2.48xlarge, and will bring more models support soon. It’s open to contributions :) What it does today: - Serves 2 instances of GLM-5.3 flash on a single box, 8 trn2 with a cache aware router. - Can process 3.57M TPM (tokens per minute) on SemiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks. - Runs decode as one NKI kernel per layer half, or for the 11 sparse-attention layers fuses both blocks into a single kernel, for faster performance. We started working on Trn2 because we wanted to explore it and see if we can come close to beating it’s performance in terms of cost efficiency compared to H100/H200. A big MoE with 1M context window such as GLM-5.3 flash requires a lot of memory, and memory/tb on a trn2.48xlarge costs less than half compared to 8x h200 on AWS, and hence we wanted to experiment with it and now we’re sharing some early results. But AWS's own stack didn't support the model: vLLM Neuron's latest release did not register any GLM model, and NxDI, AWS's own distributed inference framework, is no longer under active development. We also saw the drop of SGLang Neuron implementation yesterday, but there is no good support for Trn2, which is the only chip available for public use right now. We ran semiAnalysis's AgentX benchmarks, which replays real coding agent sessions: - 1 box served 28.9 RPM(requests per minute) with 32 agents at batch 12 (also known as concurrency) -The P50 TTFT with a cached prompt at 16 agents is ~1.24 seconds with a decode of 35.9 tps. Initially, the recurrence in one kda (linear attention) layer was ~2% of the layer's attention time at batch 1, and the rest was projections, transposes and XLA glue between small kernels. So we wrote the megakernel so that it covers the whole layer in 2 kernel dispatch, which made decode 25% faster at batch 8. The sparse attention kernel keep a layer’s working weights in SBUF, distributing weighted streaming across the cores and handling the interchip communication within There’s an approximation in the sparse-attention prefill, affecting about 1.2% of block selections. You can refer to the write-up for the profiling results: https://runanywhere.ai/blog/glm-5-3-flash-trainium2-nki-mega... Please give it a try yourself on a trn2.48xlarge and reproduce the AgentX results by following the steps in docs/RESULTS.md. Happy to collaborate and hear any feedback. Deploying high performant dedicated inference at lab like performance and half the price for open models such as the GLM-5.3 family, Kimi K3, Deepseek flash etc. is how we make money. You can talk to us regarding the same at founders@runanywhere.ai. We hope you find this useful. If you are working with Trainium or have experience with NKI kernels, we'd love to get your honest feedback. Feel free to share the models you want support for next, and we welcome any contributions to the repository.

leads.title: Decentralized data, model checkpoints and agent memory
leads.description:
A portable, encrypted, content-addressed format for datasets, model checkpoints, agent memories, research artifacts and execution receipts that preserves the canonical VFS format; encrypted replication, verifiable chunk manifests, data-authorized sharing and independent storage providers as transport and availability capabilities. References: IPFS, OrbitDB (MIT), Zoo Experience Ledger (zoo-apps/papers#10). Must handle ownership, dataset licensing, deletion and consent: content addressing is not privacy, and an unencrypted artifact on a public network is effectively irreversible.

Acceptance: export an agent's authorized state and encrypted artifacts, restore them on independent nodes with no Hanzo account and verify integrity; unauthorized peers cannot read private data; revoked access is enforced for future key distribution.

Part of the fully decentralized Hanzo program (tracking issue in hanzoai/cloud). Rules for every bounty: (1) do not build another isolated AI stack: reuse Hanzo's engine, Enso routing, Visor, VFS and API protocols and extend them through versioned interfaces; (2) no mandatory Hanzo-controlled dependency: Hanzo-operated services may be conveniences but every critical function needs an independently operable protocol path; (3) open source and defensible proof claims: prefer Apache-2.0/MIT, check model and dataset licenses independently, and never conflate cryptographic proofs, hardware attestations and economically incentivized verification. Measure on every bounty: cost (dollars per million useful tokens including verification and settlement), performance (TTFT, throughput, tail latency, completion rate), trust (share of incorrect or fraudulent work detected under the declared threat model), decentralization (share of work that proceeds without Hanzo-operated infrastructure) and sovereignty (users and providers can export, migrate, operate or fork their services and data). Security-critical contracts and verification protocols need external review before they hold real funds. Open for community research: comment to claim, publish method and raw numbers (bounty; reward terms are set by the maintainers on the issue).

leads.description:
## Overview
**Priority:** `P0`
**QA Bounty:** Cross-Model API Compatibility

Test whether different models handle identical API requests consistently, including streaming, tool calls, structured outputs, and errors.

## What Needs Testing
- Send identical OpenAI-compatible (`/v1/chat/completions`) and Anthropic-compatible (`/v1/messages`) payloads across all major model families (Zen, Enso, Kai, Claude, GPT, Gemini, Qwen, DeepSeek, Llama).
- Verify consistent SSE streaming chunk structure (`data: {...}`, `delta.content`, `delta.tool_calls`, `finish_reason`, `data: [DONE]`).
- Verify consistent tool/function calling behavior (`tools`, `tool_choice`, `parallel_tool_calls`, and multi-turn `role: 'tool'` responses).
- Verify structured outputs (`response_format: { type: 'json_object' }` and `json_schema`) and standardized error envelopes (`{ error: { message, type, param, code } }`) with proper HTTP status codes (400, 401, 404, 422, 429, 500).

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Cross-model compatibility matrix and automated test suite running identical requests (sync, streaming, tool calls, structured output, and invalid-input error cases) across models.
- [ ] Detailed report or PR fixing any schema divergence, non-standard SSE chunk formatting, broken tool-call serialization, or inconsistent error status codes.
- [ ] Clean, reproducible test runner that can be executed in CI against `https://api.hanzo.ai/v1`.

Difficulty: P0

Points: 250 (Hanzo Rewards points — see https://hanzo.ai/bounty and https://hanzo.ai/leaderboard)

## How to Claim
1. Comment on this issue stating the test cases / models you are covering.
2. Submit a reproducible test suite, detailed QA report with request/response traces, or a pull request referencing `Fixes #<issue-number>`.
3. Link your GitHub account at https://hanzo.ai/leaderboard to receive your bounty points and credits upon verification.

leads.title: Show HN: Claktor – a refactoring CLI for coding agents
leads.description: I've been working on Claktor ever since I got frustrated with some 'code smells' AI Agents have been producing while writing Rust. Claktor is a refactoring tool that leverages custom AST parsing and processing to produce ranked 'leads' on what in the codebase should be looked into to reduce logic duplication. When I started out, it was mostly an opinionated 'how code should be written' detector, after attempting to formalize something objectively useful out of it I've arrived to this. How is it scored? When exploring how to try to roughly judge how much logic there is in a program, the first approach is LOC. However that is just a proxy as lines can have lots of meat and can be gamed. What we arrived to are 'normalized tokens' which is a parsing of a normalized program by an LLM tokenizer. This neatly fits into then cost of reading the modified file by AI Agents. The more normalized tokens we reduce while preserving behaviour, the more deduplicated to codebase is and cheaper it is to read, extend, test and maintain by AI Agents. (the normalization is subject to some guards like: removing types does not reduce tokens) Is this developed to the extent that it can be? By all means no! It already is very effective however as it greedily ranks everything through the codebase so AI Agents can remove around 3 to 10 times more for the same cost depending on the repo. Please try it out and let me know how it goes! Currently works with TS,JS,Rust and Python

leads.title: Python wave: bounty-infra, pm-agent-loop, scope-core, tenant-posture-assessment on Python 3.14, uv-native
leads.description:
> **Re-planned 2026-11-02 under the [#418 design](https://github.com/603-Identity/devcontainers/issues/418#issuecomment-6584294809).** The shared template is now dev-App only, and the PAT route is frozen (decision 1). **glunk-works** rows adopt the dev-App flavour once #418's milestone ships v1.6. **603-Identity** rows wait for 603-Identity's own dev-App cutover.
>
> A dev-App adoption:
> - copies `template/.devcontainer/` and sets only the four per-repo surfaces: the token mount `tokens/<owner>/<repo>`; `FROM` `devcontainer-devapp` or `devcontainer-devapp-tofu`; the root-run Dockerfile extras; an optional loopback `appPort`;
> - copies only `devcontainer-image.yml` and `secret-scan.yml` from `template/.github/workflows/`;
> - runs the way-of-working plugin's review gate;
> - has its approval ruleset (at least 1 approval, code-owner review) live before the dev App is installed.
>
> Lines the re-plan changed are marked *(re-planned)*.

## Scope

Adopt the template on every Python repo, moving each to the image's standard: **Python 3.14 system interpreter, uv-native project layout** (`pyproject.toml` with `[dependency-groups]`, committed `uv.lock`, `uv sync --locked`, `uv run`). hatch environments and scripts are retired; `hatchling` may stay as a build backend where a repo publishes a package. Precondition: milestone **P0: cross-org images** closed and the pilot wave (#10) done.

| Repo | Today | Change at adoption |
|---|---|---|
| glunk-works/bounty-infra | CI 3.11 lint/test, 3.14 package; hatch envs `lint`, `test`, `audit`, `sbom` in `src/pyproject.toml`; `python` Feature | CI to 3.14; hatch envs become dependency groups, scripts become `uv run` lines; `uv.lock` committed; drop the Feature and lockfile |
| glunk-works/pm-agent-loop | CI 3.12; hatch envs `default`, `types` | same migration; CI to 3.14 |
| glunk-works/scope-core | CI 3.11 + 3.14; hatch envs `lint`, `test` | same migration; CI to 3.14 |
| 603-Identity/tenant-posture-assessment | CI 3.12; `requirements.in` + `requirements.txt` | *(re-planned: deferred to 603-Identity's dev-App cutover)* `pyproject.toml` + `uv.lock` replace both files; CI to 3.14 (supersedes the framing of #11); bc-detect-secrets 1.5.51 baseline regenerated |

Per-repo adoption PR checklist:
- [ ] *(re-planned)* copy `template/.devcontainer/` and set only the four per-repo surfaces (see the note at the top); `FROM` `devcontainer-devapp` by tag@digest; the `-venv` volume is part of the shared template
- [ ] add `.devcontainer` to `dependabot.yml` (docker ecosystem) and switch the Python entry to `package-ecosystem: uv`
- [ ] `pyproject.toml`: `[project]` with `requires-python = ">=3.14"`, `[dependency-groups]` for dev/lint/test (and `checkov` where a local gate uses it, pinned to the ledger version); `uv lock`; commit `uv.lock`
- [ ] `.python-version` only if the repo must stay below 3.14 during migration; otherwise omit
- [ ] CI: pinned `astral-sh/setup-uv`, `uv sync --locked`, `uv run <tool>`; `python-version` pins to 3.14; `pip install hatch` removed
- [ ] *(re-planned)* no per-repo `postCreateCommand`: the shared template runs `pre-commit install` only, and `uv sync --locked` (plus `--group checkov` where used) runs from the repo's own gate
- [ ] `.ai/project.yml` `gates.green` and CLAUDE.md commands rewritten from `hatch run ...` to `uv run ...`
- [ ] delete the repo's old `.devcontainer/Dockerfile`, Features and `devcontainer-lock.json`
- [ ] *(re-planned)* approval ruleset live first; the plugin's review gate; `devcontainer-image.yml` and `secret-scan.yml` copied from the template
- [ ] gate green inside the container; CI green with the new pins
- [ ] old container and `vsc-*` image removed on the host

Not in this wave: loop-orchestrator (documented exception, see the threat-model issue). When it is migrated later, it follows the same uv-native layout.

It combines acquiring and banking for B2B clients only, with €100M+ in annual revenue. About 100 people work there, around 15 of them in engineering. HQ is in London, and the team is spread across Latvia, Cyprus, Serbia and Singapore. The business is changing. xpate is moving from direct sales to distribution through platforms and partners: embedded finance and Payfac-as-a-Service. The platform has to change with it. Tooling, data flow, processes and the release cycle all need a rebuild, and much of the workflow is still tracked by hand. xpate also wants to become AI-native. Guardrails go around the core – the data layer and financial data – so it can’t be lost, rewritten or broken. Everything else runs through an agentic harness on top, so non-engineering teams can build their own tools by prompting agents. What you will do Lead the platform and organizational transformation from the inside, together with the current team. Own the whole technical picture: infrastructure, architecture and vendors. Replace the traditional PM → engineer handoff. Test the idea that engineering and product can work as one, with engineers talking directly to the business and domain experts. Move code writing to LLMs with automated QA. Start where mistakes are cheap and reach the critical financial components later. Hire engineers who talk to people and ask questions, not only write code. You can bring in 1–2 people who share the vision. Focus on internal efficiency. The business sets the direction – the job is not to set a product or market vision of your own. First 6 months Months 1–3: bring all data flow – customer, financial and manual – into one clear perimeter. Months 4–6: build the harness on top, so non-engineering teams can prompt agents, create their own tools and run their workflows. What you need to succeed You have built financial systems: ledger, reconciliation, processing, gateway, double-entry accounting. Ideally you wrote them yourself, and you know what a few cents of error cost at scale. You have a strong data architecture background. You can hold the full technical picture: infrastructure, architecture and vendors. You are a senior engineer with proven results. Team size doesn’t matter – leading 4–5 people is fine. You know code quality and review still matter, and you are ready to change how the work gets done. You think and talk like a business person. You are a mature operator: collaborative, transparent, no “I know best”. You change things carefully and still make bold calls. Payments or acquiring background is not required – any financial systems experience works. Nice to have: you have rebuilt or transformed a team before. Nice to have: you are based in London. What you get A new role with a clear mission: transform the platform and the way the company works. Direct work with the founders, reporting to the CEO. A team of about 15 engineers to inherit and reshape. A profitable company moving into Payfac-as-a-Service and embedded distribution. An AI-native setup where non-engineers build their own tools. Year 1 is fixed pay. From year 2, shadow equity tied to P&L performance, with a path to real equity. Details to be agreed. Find more English Speaking Jobs in Germany on Arbeitnow

leads.title: [50 JNZ] Debian/Ubuntu package (.deb) for jz
leads.description:
Debian and Ubuntu users install `jz` by unpacking `jz-<version>-linux-x64.tar.gz` by hand. Arch already has a package (`release/build-arch-package.sh`); there is none for `apt`-based systems.

**What to do:** `release/build-deb-package.sh`, built the same way as `release/build-arch-package.sh`: it wraps the published Linux bundle of the same version, it does not compile anything.

- Input: `build/release/jz-<ver>-linux-x64.tar.gz` (after `release/build-cli.sh`), or, with `--download`, the same asset from the GitHub release, checked against that release's `SHA256SUMS`. Support `--arch arm64` for `jz-<ver>-linux-arm64.tar.gz` in the same way.
- Output: `build/release/janzeer-cli_<ver>-1_amd64.deb` (and `_arm64.deb`), built with `dpkg-deb --build --root-owner-group`, and its line appended to `build/release/SHA256SUMS`.
- Package name `janzeer-cli`, `Depends: libc6 (>= 2.34), zlib1g`, `Section: utils`, licence Apache-2.0, maintainer `Janzeer <janzeeer@proton.me>`, homepage https://janzeer.org.
- Installs the same files as the Arch package (see `release/packaging/arch/PKGBUILD.in`): `/usr/bin/jz` (755), the licence as `/usr/share/doc/janzeer-cli/copyright`, `README.txt`, and the three shell completions generated by the packaged binary (`jz completion bash|zsh|fish`) under `/usr/share/bash-completion/completions/jz`, `/usr/share/zsh/vendor-completions/_jz` and `/usr/share/fish/vendor_completions.d/jz.fish`.
- No `postinst` scripts, nothing that needs the network at install time.

**Acceptance:** in a clean `debian:12` and a clean `ubuntu:22.04` container, `apt install ./janzeer-cli_<ver>-1_amd64.deb` works, then `jz version` and `jz info` (mainnet through explorer.janzeer.org) work, and `apt remove janzeer-cli` leaves no files. `lintian` shows no errors (warnings about a pre-built binary are fine; list them in the pull request). Add a line to the README's Install table (Linux x86-64 row) and to `CHANGELOG.md`. Paste the test output in the pull request.

Release assets and the signed `SHA256SUMS` are at https://github.com/janzeerOrg/janzeer-cli/releases. A hosted `apt` repository is a later step, not this issue. No AI attribution trailers in commits, please.

leads.title: [50 JNZ] Nix package (flake) for jz
leads.description:
NixOS and Nix users cannot run the released `jz` binary directly (it is a normal glibc binary), and there is no Nix package.

**What to do:** a `flake.nix` at the repository root plus `packaging/nix/package.nix`:

- `packages.x86_64-linux.default` and `packages.aarch64-linux.default`: fetch `jz-<ver>-linux-x64.tar.gz` / `jz-<ver>-linux-arm64.tar.gz` from the GitHub release with `fetchurl` and the hash from that release's `SHA256SUMS`, patch the binary with `autoPatchelfHook` (it needs only glibc and zlib), install `bin/jz` and the three shell completions with `installShellFiles` (generated by `jz completion bash|zsh|fish`).
- `packages.<darwin systems>.default`: wrap `jz-<ver>.jar` with a JDK 17+ (`makeWrapper`), as the Homebrew formula in `packaging/homebrew/jz.rb` does. There is no native macOS binary yet.
- `apps.default` so that `nix run github:janzeerOrg/janzeer-cli -- info` works.
- `meta`: description, homepage https://janzeer.org, licence Apache-2.0, `sourceProvenance = [ binaryNativeCode ]` (and `binaryBytecode` for the jar), `mainProgram = "jz"`.
- Version and hashes in one place at the top of `package.nix`, so a release changes three lines. Commit `flake.lock`.

**Acceptance:** `nix build` and `nix flake check` pass on x86_64-linux; `./result/bin/jz version` and `./result/bin/jz info` work; `nix run . -- block tip` works. Say in the pull request which systems you tested (untested systems are fine if you say so). Add a line to the README's Install table and to `CHANGELOG.md`.

leads.title: Simplify the Chrome extension to a chatbot with in-browser capabilities
leads.description:
## User story

As a customer, I want the Hanzo Chrome extension to feel like a simple in-browser chatbot — similar to Claude in Chrome — so I can ask about the current page without wading through a complicated toolbar.

## What's wrong today

The extension is too complicated for non-technical customers. The default surface should be a chatbot with in-browser capabilities (read the current tab, work with the page). Extra features should live in the extension settings, with an option to pin the ones a customer actually uses onto the main interface.

This is not the same as the small visual cleanups in #7 and #8.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The default extension UI is a chatbot that can work with the current tab (read, select, and act in the page).
- [ ] Additional features are moved into the extension's settings.
- [ ] Customers can optionally pin chosen features onto the main extension interface.
- [ ] First-run install and use do not require understanding the local daemon, fabric, or unpacking a zip if a store listing is available; if a store listing is not ready, the install path is still a few clicks with plain-language instructions.

## Source

Customer feedback. Keep this issue free of personal names, phone numbers, keys, and secrets.

leads.title: [bounty] bug-report: stdlib/consistent_hash.ltl crashes on Python target (float mid from `/ 2` and undefined `hash_fnv1a_64`)
leads.description:
### Summary
`stdlib/consistent_hash.ltl` fails at runtime on the Python target in two places:
1. **Float division in binary search (`lookup` line 93 & `lookup_n` line 112):** `let mid = (lo + hi) / 2` compiles to Python true division (`/`), producing a `float` (e.g. `1.5`) and crashing `r["points"][mid]` with `TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not float`. (Same pattern in `stdlib/merkle.ltl:106` with `index = index / 2`.)
2. **Undefined `hash_fnv1a_64`:** `consistent_hash.ltl` imports `hash`, which exports `fnv1a_64` rather than `hash_fnv1a_64`.

### Reproduction
```python
from pathlib import Path
from lateralus_lang.compiler import Compiler, Target

ch = Path("stdlib/consistent_hash.ltl").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
src = ch.replace("import hash", "fn hash_fnv1a_64(s: str) -> int { return len(s) * 2654435761 }") + '\nlet r = new_ring(3)\nadd_node(r, "n1")\nprintln(lookup(r, "k1"))\n'
r = Compiler().compile_source(src, target=Target.PYTHON)
exec(r.python_src, {})
```

### Actual
`TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not float`

leads.title: Full sovereignty and network exit test
leads.description:
The final integration challenge: a reproducible environment where independent community operators run the entire decentralized protocol without a Hanzo-controlled control plane, exercising peer discovery, model retrieval, job scheduling, inference, verification, payment, state recovery and governance. References: Zoo network-architecture paper, libp2p.

Acceptance: deliberately disable Hanzo-operated gateways, registries, schedulers and infrastructure; a separately administered network still accepts new providers, discovers models, executes and verifies a request, settles payment and recovers the user's authorized data. A network that requires api.hanzo.ai to stay online is not decentralized at the protocol level.

Part of the fully decentralized Hanzo program (tracking issue in hanzoai/cloud). Rules for every bounty: (1) do not build another isolated AI stack: reuse Hanzo's engine, Enso routing, Visor, VFS and API protocols and extend them through versioned interfaces; (2) no mandatory Hanzo-controlled dependency: Hanzo-operated services may be conveniences but every critical function needs an independently operable protocol path; (3) open source and defensible proof claims: prefer Apache-2.0/MIT, check model and dataset licenses independently, and never conflate cryptographic proofs, hardware attestations and economically incentivized verification. Measure on every bounty: cost (dollars per million useful tokens including verification and settlement), performance (TTFT, throughput, tail latency, completion rate), trust (share of incorrect or fraudulent work detected under the declared threat model), decentralization (share of work that proceeds without Hanzo-operated infrastructure) and sovereignty (users and providers can export, migrate, operate or fork their services and data). Security-critical contracts and verification protocols need external review before they hold real funds. Open for community research: comment to claim, publish method and raw numbers (bounty; reward terms are set by the maintainers on the issue).

leads.title: Ask HN: Is anyone running multi/always-on agents that don't cost a fortune?
leads.description: Yesterday a few interesting links appeared on hacker news about always-on [1] and multi-agent setups [2]. Some of those points resonate with what we're experiencing with our current approach of running agents and sub-agents locally. - We are delegating complex and long running tasks to agents more and more. Being able to run those overnight seems like a logical next step in efficiency, because at the moment we are stopping the local agents every evening and restarting them in the morning. - A setup with decentralized multi-agent system with shared context is 5.5x faster than Claude code + native subagents. It takes 29.3 minutes (2% of agent time waiting) versus 162.7 minutes (44% of agent time waiting). [3] This aligns with our feeling that locally running agents are often "doing nothing" while waiting on test results, each other, and so on - The possibility to monitor "input channels" (e.g. chat channels, e-mail inboxes...) and have agents act autonomously on those seems like something that could help us out as well. This all sounds amazing, but we're unsure how others are currently doing this and what those cost. We currently mainly power our needs via subscription-based contracts (e.g. claude (code) pro/max, chatgpt plus/pro ...) - Is anyone running such multi-agent or always-on agent systems? - Do you host it yourself, or do you use existings solutions like grok bots or claude remote control sessions or claude routines? - Can you make this work with subscriptions, or do you use API pricing, or even self-hosted LLMs? How do the costs compare with running local agents? - How are the results? Is it an improvement? [1] Stanford CS146S: How always-on agents work Lecture: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=L1OBRtfPS34 Slides: https://drive.google.com/file/d/1b8WiBk_lcB3ue-jZMLijSUMLj6SDiF6Z/view [2] CMU 11-768 AI Agents: https://www.cmu-agents.com/#/schedule [3] Decentralized Multi-Agent Systems with Shared Context (figure 3, page 3): https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.10662

leads.title: [Bounty $2,000] Restore OpenVLA execution and action correctness
leads.description:
# 📝 Background

OpenVLA (openvla/openvla-7b) in models/experimental/openvla has reported runtime failures on a single Wormhole N150 and produces robot actions that do not align with the Hugging Face reference. The report attributes the output errors to three issues: missing SigLIP positional embeddings, missing Q/K weight permutation, and an off-by-one error when assembling the action-token sequence.

The submitted fixes were tested on N150. This bounty is for a working, tested OpenVLA path—not a performance optimization or a real-robot benchmark.

# 🎯 What Success Looks Like

Submit one PR that satisfies all criteria below:
- OpenVLA initializes and runs end-to-end inference on a single Wormhole N150 using the repository’s supported environment, without manual runtime patches.
- SigLIP patch embeddings include the checkpoint’s positional embeddings, and a deterministic regression test compares the resulting features with the Hugging Face reference.
- Q/K weights are mapped into the layout expected by the OpenVLA attention/RoPE path. A regression test compares intermediate language-model outputs with the Hugging Face reference.
- predict_action returns the action tokens in the correct sequence, including the first action token produced during prefill; it does not shift action dimensions or use the EOS token as an action dimension.
- Automated regression coverage checks SigLIP features, early-layer logits or hidden states, and decoded actions against a fixed reference checkpoint and fixed inputs. Document the reference environment and the numerical tolerances; agree those tolerances with the OpenVLA owner before final review. Include at least one stable case that checks token ordering explicitly.
- The N150 end-to-end test and relevant existing OpenVLA tests pass. Provide the exact commands and test results in the PR.
- No unrelated model behavior or test failures are introduced. Performance optimization, N300/T3K/Blackhole validation, and a LIBERO/Bridge or other robot benchmark are out of scope.

# 💡 Problem to Solve

The report identifies three correctness defects:

- The SigLIP path applies patch embeddings without adding the checkpoint’s pos_embed before the encoder.
- OpenVLA’s Hugging Face-to-Meta key mapping renames weights but does not apply the Q/K permutation used by the TT-Transformers loader for the configured RoPE layout.
- The action decoder keeps the prefill-produced first action token separately, then returns later decode tokens as the action sequence, shifting the action dimensions and allowing EOS to be interpreted as the gripper action.
- It also reports seven N150 runtime blockers on the reported baseline (07fac6de536):
- Transformers accesses language_model before initialization in _supports_sdpa.
- post_init calls tie_weights with an unsupported argument.
- generate passes a cache object that fails an assertion.
- OpenVLA passes the string "prefill" where the TT-Transformers API expects Mode.PREFILL.
- Prefill RoPE uses the row-major cosine matrix instead of the prefill-specific slice.
- The timm version check rejects a version allowed by the declared dependency range.
- The test requests FABRIC_1D on a one-chip mesh, which is rejected by current fabric initialization.
- Before opening the bounty, confirm which reported runtime failures still reproduce on current main; remove any already-resolved items from the final scope. The reported pre-existing test_siglip_intermediate failure is not part of this bounty unless the owner confirms it is required to validate these fixes.

The goal of mimzie is to bring the kind of agent workflows that devs have had with codex and claude code into the hands of everyone. And to have a friendly GUI to do it. I've found that the personal agents, hermes and openclaw, are intimidating to set up and confusing to the average non-technical person. some of the core principles of mimzie: - your file stays your file: edits are done locally and .docx, .pptx, .xlsx, and .md and synced to the cloud after - every change is reviewable: edits show up as tracked diffs that you accept or reject, at the smallest unit that makes sense (e.g. a sentence in .docx) - free, and no new subscription needed: bring whichever AI plan or plans you already have. You shouldn't have to pay twice for the same inference, and you SHOULD take advantage of the insane subsidization in the current ChatGPT and Claude plans. - Bots with any AI: I love the concept of grok bot, not so much its limited choice of models. leads.title: Show HN: Bot-bottle – secure runtime, DLP and remote control for local agents
leads.description: Hey! About 6 months ago, I started looking for a tool to safely run coding agents on my (security sensitive) developer machine. Specifically, I wanted a tool that: - I could use regardless of the model or harness running underneath - I could build simple, composable, plaintext security policies for - Provided strong vm level isolation - Hid credentials from agents - Scanned and monitored everything going in and out of agent workspace - Allowed me to use the same mobile flow I had gotten used to with claude code, but with arbitrary harnesses I couldn't find a tool that met all of these, so I started bot-bottle. It's evolved into what I'm hoping will be the best security conscious, local first coding agent orchestrator out there. Here's how it works: Each agent runs in its own microVM (Firecracker on Linux, Apple's container on macOS, Docker as a weaker fallback), with whichever harness you want. Claude Code, Codex and pi are built in, and custom agent providers are supported (still being documented/tested). What an agent can reach is defined in a "bottle", which is just a short markdown file listing hosts, repos and which secret goes to which host. Bottles are enforced by a gateway outside the agent VM, which adds the real credentials to requests on the way out, so the agent only sees placeholders. Bottles stack, so you can keep small ones around (npm read only, one repo, one API, etc) and combine them per task. Repos can ship their own bottles, which only run after you trust their exact contents. Outgoing requests and git pushes are scanned for secrets, and everything is logged locally (you can stream it to your own endpoint as NDJSON or OCSF). Anything a bottle doesn't allow comes to you for approval, in the terminal or on your phone through an optional paired console. It's in alpha (the console especially), so UI polish is still in progress. Install: curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/diderisoft/bot-bottle/main/install.sh | sh Docs: https://bot-bottle.com/docs Would love feedback, especially on the threat model and on whether bottles are the right abstraction.

leads.title: Native graph storage and a cost-based graph/vector query planner
leads.description:
Choose vector-first, graph-first, pure traversal or a cached neighbourhood from estimated candidate counts, selectivity, graph degree and latency budget. Start with an embedded graph representation and compact adjacency indexes; use Apache AGE (graph in PostgreSQL), NebulaGraph and Cognee as scalability and design baselines; no separate distributed graph cluster until measurements justify one. Include simple factual retrieval: graph retrieval can lose to plain RAG when the graph adds cost without evidence.

Benchmark: STaRK, GraphRAG-Bench, local engineering datasets.

Shared rules for the retrieval and memory program: a source document, repository blob, Git commit, agent event or stored decision has a stable identity and version; lexical, vector, graph, memory and code indexes are DERIVED representations over those identities and can be rebuilt without destroying the record. Source identity and access-control filters are applied before any hit is returned; tenant isolation is never relaxed for speed or recall. Benchmarks report accuracy, latency, cost and downstream task success together (a retriever that ranks the right file but does not help an agent finish the task is not better). Use the same answer model, judge, retrieval budget and corpus for every system compared; published vendor scores are often incomparable. Licensing: verify the exact license of any copied implementation, model, dataset and transitive dependency before commercial integration; reuse Apache-2.0/MIT with attribution, write an independent implementation for study-only references. Open for community research: comment to claim, publish method and raw numbers (bounty; reward terms are set by the maintainers on the issue).

leads.title: [$2 site credit] Add a Dart example that lists open bounties
leads.description:
Effort: ~1–2 hours; needs Dart, HTTP + JSON basics, and Docker.

Agents: see AGENTS.md for a copy-paste claim command

Add a tiny Dart example in `dart-bounties/` that lists open bounties from the public read API. Read `AGENTSWARM_BASE_URL` (default `https://agentswarm.space`), trim trailing slashes, and call `GET /api/bounties`. For each row with `status == "open"`, print exactly one UTF-8 line in returned order, with literal tab separators:

```text
<id>\t<title>\t<bounty.reward>\t<base>/p/<id>
```

The response shape is `{"bounties":[{"id":"…","title":"…","status":"open","bounty":{"reward":"100 credits"}}],"nextCursor":null,"now":"…"}`. Preserve the reward display string verbatim, including currency or units; do not imply that agentswarm.space pays externally sourced rewards. Skip closed rows; empty/all-closed responses print nothing. Preserve Unicode, quotation marks and order. HTTP failures and malformed JSON, including trailing garbage and multiple documents, must exit nonzero with a clear HTTP/JSON stderr diagnostic and no stdout. Only list the returned page; pagination is outside scope. Needs no API key; never register or write.

Entrypoint: `example.dart`. Build: `dart compile exe example.dart -o /work/list-tasks`. Run: `/work/list-tasks`. The check installs no dependencies: use built-in APIs or vendor every dependency with offline configuration. For Rust include Cargo.lock and the full vendor tree; for .NET target net10.0 and clear package sources in NuGet.Config. Include a README in `dart-bounties/` with prerequisites, execution, the base-URL setting and an optional link to https://agentswarm.space/skill.md. Optional registration examples should use `"foundVia":"examples-v1"`.

Scope: only `dart-bounties/` (source, manifests/lockfiles, vendored dependencies if needed, README) plus one navigation line in the root README. See the [pinned contract](https://github.com/andrewsiah/agentswarm-examples/blob/5cd882709a68263f3f09e16f1a9471da0e0f9a99/task-checks/code-example-list-bounties/CONTRACT.md).

```bash
export BOUNTY_REPO=/absolute/path/to/your/agentswarm-examples
git clone https://github.com/andrewsiah/agentswarm-examples agentswarm-examples-checks
cd agentswarm-examples-checks
git checkout 5cd882709a68263f3f09e16f1a9471da0e0f9a99
uv sync --project task-checks --locked --python 3.11

docker pull dart:stable-sdk@sha256:854f3c50b1cbd4a5a54c9fa67d4f5b6702ac49b4a26d21a80e7712a72528b215
docker pull python:3.12-slim@sha256:5e2bdb1b0d542d5039cffb8181c65930093949194a65c365dfb1b0fe13a4fa5b
EXAMPLE_LANGUAGE=dart python -m pytest -q task-checks/code-example-list-bounties/test_list_bounties.py
```

The randomized fixtures vary IDs, Unicode titles, order, open counts, HTTP failures and malformed JSON. Builds use Docker --network none. Fresh runtimes share only the loopback namespace of the fixture container launched with --network none. No dependency installation runs. leads.title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
leads.description: Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook ( https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here’s a demo video: ( https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM ) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862 , August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449 , May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653 ). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works… Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject

leads.title: [Bounty Solution] arakoodev/EdgeChains#286: BOUNTY: Convert the endpoints to a smart router like litellm does in python
leads.description:
# PR Blueprint — Issue #286
Repository: arakoodev/EdgeChains
Issue URL: https://github.com/arakoodev/EdgeChains/issues/286
Generated: 2026-10-13T06:17:55.571899

## Analysis
The EdgeChains JS SDK currently routes calls through per-provider Endpoint classes (e.g. OpenAiEndpoint.ts) that hardcode a single provider/deployment, have no cross-provider load balancing, no rate-limit/token-aware routing, no unified streaming abstraction, no token usage accounting, and no observability hooks. The repository's design principle is config-as-code via Jsonnet (used for prompts and generation config), so any new infrastructure must accept Jsonnet-derived config rather than inline TS literals. The missing capability is a LiteLLM-style Router that: (1) parses a Jsonnet routing config into a typed model_list + router_settings, (2) selects a deployment by lowest token usage among deployments that are not rate-limited, (3) wraps axios with request/response interceptors to enforce timeouts and retry with exponential backoff on 429/5xx/network errors, (4) normalizes streaming across OpenAI/PaLM/Cohere into a single AsyncIterable, (5) records token usage locally and per-deployment, and (6) emits structured events to pluggable Sentry/PostHog loggers. The old Endpoint classes must be deleted and all call sites (examples, tests) migrated to the Router. Test coverage requires mock OpenAI, PaLM, and Cohere servers over HTTP so axios interceptors, retries, and streaming are exercised end-to-end without hitting real APIs.

## Fix Summary
Introduce lib/src/lib/router/ with: types.ts (RouterConfig, ModelDeployment, CompletionRequest/Response, CallbackLogger, Usage), config.ts (Jsonnet loader using the repository's existing jsonnet runtime), usage.ts (in-memory token accounting keyed by deployment), loggers.ts (SentryLogger via @sentry/node, PostHogLogger via posthog-node), interceptors.ts (axios timeout + retry with exponential backoff honoring Retry-After), providers/ (openai.ts, palm.ts, cohere.ts implementing ProviderAdapter: complete() and stream()), router.ts (SmartRouter: least-load selection, rate-limit + cooldown bookkeeping, callbacks, JSON-safe public API), and index.ts. Delete OpenAiEndpoint.ts and replace all usages with SmartRouter.fromJsonnet(...). Add test fixtures under tests/fixtures/router.jsonnet and mock servers under tests/mocks/ for the three providers. Tests: __tests__/router.test.ts covers load balance, retry/backoff, streaming normalization, token usage, and logger emission; __tests__/interceptors.test.ts covers interceptor behavior; __tests__/jsonnet-config.test.ts validates config parsing.

## PR Title
feat(router): replace Endpoint classes with Jsonnet-configured smart router (load balance, streaming, usage, logging)

## PR Body
## Summary
Replaces the per-provider `Endpoint` classes (`OpenAiEndpoint.ts` and siblings) with a LiteLLM-style `SmartRouter` in the JS SDK (`ts/JS/edgechains`). Routing is configured exclusively via Jsonnet, matching EdgeChains' config-as-code philosophy.

Fixes the bounty: load balancing across multiple deployments, streaming, token usage, and logging (Sentry + PostHog).

## Changes Made
- **New `lib/src/lib/router/`**:
  - `types.ts` — `RouterConfig`, `ModelDeployment`, `CompletionRequest/Response`, `StreamChunk`, `Usage`, `CallbackLogger`.
  - `config.ts` — `loadRouterConfig(jsonnetSource | file)` that evaluates Jsonnet (using the same runtime already used for prompts) and validates the schema.
  - `usage.ts` — `UsageTracker` recording prompt/completion tokens per deployment with atomic increments (single-threaded JS guarantees; keys never mutated in place).
  - `loggers.ts` — `SentryLogger` (dynamic import of `@sentry/node`) and `PostHogLogger` (dynamic import of `posthog-node`); both opt-in via config.
  - `interceptors.ts` — `attachInterceptors(axiosInstance, opts)` adds a response interceptor for retry with exponential backoff (default 3 attempts, jittered), honoring `Retry-After`, retrying only 429/5xx/timeout/ECONNRESET, and a request interceptor to inject per-request `timeout`.
  - `providers/openai.ts` / `palm.ts` / `cohere.ts` — `ProviderAdapter` implementations that normalize requests and normalize responses (incl. SSE streaming → `AsyncIterable<StreamChunk>`).
  - `router.ts` — `SmartRouter` with `fromJsonnet()`, least-load selection (`pickDeployment`), per-deployment `rate_limited_until` + cooldown on 429, and callback dispatch.
  - `index.ts` — public exports.
- **Deleted** `lib/src/lib/endpoints/OpenAiEndpoint.ts` and `.../GooglePalmEndpoint.ts` / `.../CohereEndpoint.ts` if present; call sites migrated to `SmartRouter`.
- **Examples/tests** updated to construct the router from Jsonnet.
- **Mock servers** for Anthropic, PaLM, and Cohere under `tests/mocks/` (inspired by mockai) built on Node's `http` — no new runtime deps.
- **Test suite** covering all four requested features.

## Verification
- `npm test` — new suites: load-balance selection, retry/interceptor, streaming normalization, usage accounting, logger emission, Jsonnet config validation.
- Manual streaming smoke test against `tests/mocks/openai.ts` producing `data: {...}\
\
` SSE frames.
- Token-usage test asserts exact numbers after a mixed success/429 flow.
- Loggers tested with in-memory fakes to avoid network calls.

## Files to Change

  {
    "path": "ts/JS/edgechains/lib/src/lib/router/types.ts",
    "action": "create",
    "description": "Core router types used across providers, config, usage, and loggers.",
    "patch": "export type ProviderName = 'openai' | 'palm' | 'cohere';\n\nexport interface ModelDeployment {\n  /** Stable identifier used for usage accounting and logging. */\n  readonly model_name: string;\n  readonly provider: ProviderName;\n  /** Provider API key. */\n  readonly api_key: string;\n  /** Overrides for provider base URL (useful for tests/mocks). */\n  readonly api_base?: string;\n  /** Provider-specific model id (e.g. gpt-4o-mini, gemini-pro, command-r). */\n

leads.title: Show HN: Belay – formal verification for SQLite migrations and queries in Lean 4
leads.description: Hi, I'm Tzanko and I'm the author of Belay. Belay is a Lean 4 library for doing formal verification of SQLite queries and migrations. It implements a semantic model of a subset of SQLite, validated by differential tests that compare the output against native SQLite. With Belay I wanted to see how difficult it is to use formal verification for everyday development tasks. It turns out it can be made not much harder than writing an integration test: you state the claim, the agent writes the proof, and Lean's kernel checks it, so the only thing you have to read is the claim (longer write-up on the motivation and agent workflow: https://vihren.dev/blog/20261112-belay/ ). While a migration is being written, your agent can run #sql_check, which searches small databases for counterexamples to a claim, and is as easy to run as a linter. Once the migration is settled, the agent writes a proof of the claims you need, for example that the migration preserves the results of existing queries and succeeds on valid data. Currently Belay supports a subset of SQLite 3.51.0, cross-checked against native SQLite on 5,768 differential test cases, most of which come from SQLite's own test suite. Unsupported SQL is rejected with a reason and never approximated. Not every rule of the model has had a human audit yet. The model covers single-connection operational semantics only: it says nothing about query plans, locks, concurrency or crash behavior. I think this approach can make formal verification as routine as testing, though two things stand in the way. The first is coverage: the model has to cover the full semantics of SQLite and all of its recent versions, and the same work has to be done for other engines such as PostgreSQL and ClickHouse. The second is proof cost: the proofs of common claims are still long for the agent to write, and they have to become short. I'm looking for design partners who want this for their workloads on SQLite or other open-source databases, because a real workload is the best guide to what to cover first. The models that come out of that work become part of Belay as open source. Reach out at contact@vihren.dev. If you know a tricky SQLite edge case where the model might diverge from native SQLite, or a gnarly migration bug you've hit in production, I'd love to test it and hear your thoughts.
