leads.title: Wiki-driven development: coding agents update a wiki for you, you set direction
leads.description: My team has been working in a way we are calling calling wiki-driven development, where the wiki is written for the human, not the agent and the human uses primarily the wiki to set direction for the agent. This is different from Karparthy's LLm I'm curious whether others do something like it. Once I run several coding agents at a time, I get overwhelmed and disorganized. Every session makes decisions and raises questions, and I can't reread the transcripts. CLAUDE.md and agent memory help the agent, but they don't give me a place to see what is going on and decide. The problem gets worse with a team. So, I have the agents write a wiki, and they write it for me. As they work, they record only what is significant: decisions with who made them, when, and the option we passed over; open questions with an owner; and a short summary of where each area stands. I ask it to focus on the big picture, strategy, key architectural or business decisions. In more detail: 1. Agents do the work and update the pages it affects with what is significant: key decisions, key strategic points, open questions, and a summary of where things stand. 2. I read the wiki to understand the big picture: the key points, where we are, and what still needs to be decided. It is short enough to read. 3. I think and decide there: I settle a question, change a decision, lay out some more strategy points, or rewrite a page to say where I want to go. 4. The next session builds from the page I changed. Karpathy's LLM Wiki idea is related, but it compiles sources you collect into a knowledge base that keeps getting richer. His goal is completeness for research. Our approach is minimalistic: the pages distill way down from the agents' sessions, hold only what is significant, and exist only so I can think and decide. Spec-driven development has you write the spec up front for the agent to implement. Here the agent writes the wiki based on all the valuable detail that are in my session prompts and its response and I edit the wiki, so the document keeps up with the agents work and my job is thinking, organizing, deciding, direction. Here are some things I have learned doing this: - Organization is key for me as the human. I make the agent make a nice visual html with clickable links marketecture or architecture or business model canvas as the top page and navigate from there. I have it keep each page a page long so I actually am motivated to read stuff. - Have the decisions record the rejected options, so when someone brings a question back, the reasoning is available. We are constantly revisiting decisions as we work and learn and so this is very helpful. - The agent wants to write everything down. The criteria I give it is to only record what it would need to get back to where we are right now in terms of strategy, decisions, implementation. Its not that much. You can do the same with a CLAUDE.md that tells the agent what to record, and work in markdown files or Obsidian or Notion. We got so into this that we turned it into a free, MIT-licensed plugin for Claude Code and Codex that keeps the wiki as markdown files in your repo and lets you see the wiki in your browser locally: https://github.com/nimbalyst/nimbalyst-wiki. Do you work in this way? If so, what other things should we be doing and how have you made it work well?

leads.title: Show HN: Nomos – A Go harness that stops coding agents from cheating on tests
leads.description: Hi HN, Mark here. If you've pointed Claude Code, Cursor, or OpenCode at a codebase you care about and walked away thinking AI coding tools are a net negative, I pretty much agree with you. Left directly on a working branch, models optimize for shutting the compiler up on the current turn. Hit a tricky failure and they delete the failing assertion, return a hardcoded nil/true stub, rewrite the spec to match broken code, dump a 300-line function into the wrong package, or burn $15 of tokens editing in circles. Writing longer rules files ("IMPORTANT: NEVER DELETE TESTS") breaks down once context fills up. Starting over the summer I built Nomos: a single 28MB stripped static Go binary (CGO_ENABLED=0, Apache 2.0) that sits between your repo and whatever coding agent you already use. You run "nomos init" once and keep prompting in plain English - the agent drives the worktree, verification, and self-fix loop under the hood. Instead of trusting prompts, Nomos locks main read-only via Git hooks, separates spec/contract tasks (INT- ) from code tasks (SUB- ) in a local causal DAG (nomos task dag) so an agent can't edit the spec to excuse broken code, and isolates every task in a Git worktree (worktrees/<repo>-<task>) under a strict state machine (IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN). Throwing away a bad run is free. Before anything merges to main, "nomos verify" runs 42 in-binary structural/AST gates (~460ms full pass, ~24ms single-file via --fast-file) plus your repo's own compiler and test suite. It blocks fake shims, deleted assertions, skipped tests (t.Skip, @pytest.mark.skip, #[ignore], @Disabled, [Fact(Skip=...)]), leaked secrets, functions over 60 LOC, complexity spikes, hardcoded paths, symlinks, and nomos.yaml rubric tampering against pinned main, returning file:line fixes for the next turn. Any gate failure or panic aborts the two-phase merge before main moves. "nomos mem" stores architectural lessons locally in embedded pure-Go SQLite (mneme.db), promoting patterns only after a verified merge with a Git Notes receipt (refs/notes/nomos/releases) so failed runs don't poison memory. No cloud account, daemon, or telemetry. One fun lesson from running the PreToolUse and PostToolUse hooks against the public TraceTrial-Bench harness benchmark (arXiv:2610.32285 - summary and spec in the repo README): my first PostToolUse hook injected helpful "process failure / refusal" warnings into tool results, and it degraded native OS EACCES guardrail attribution by -39.3% because synthetic hook text polluted error channels. Compiling "nomos hook" (session-start, pre-tool, post-tool at ~4ms cold start), keeping PostToolUse silent on native channels, and moving enforcement to PreToolUse path guards plus a 3-strike identical-failure circuit-breaker recovered that -39.3% drop and lifted stateful handoff, context continuity, and guardrail tasks cleanly. Two rough edges upfront. First, while full type-checking, tests, and coverage ratchets (go test, LCOV, Cobertura XML) run via native toolchains across Go, TS/Svelte, Python, Rust, C/C++, Java/Kotlin, and C#, the fast in-binary pass uses go/ast for Go and combines a wazero WASM linear-memory cache and .scm query compiler with pure-Go multiline lexical scanners rather than bundling multi-MB per-language .wasm grammars (keeping the binary 28MB, CGO_ENABLED=0). Second, running the full IDLE -> PLAN -> EDIT -> REVIEW -> SYNC -> LEARN loop adds turn overhead, so for a 100-line weekend prototype raw vibe-coding is faster - Nomos is for repos you still have to understand six months from now. Curious how others here fence coding agents in on real repos (containers, Git hooks, jj workspaces, custom linters?), and what sneakier "make the build green" shortcuts still slip past your checks.

leads.title: Launch HN: Kino AI (YC S23) – AI media manager and video editor
leads.description: Hi HN! I'm Luke from Kino ( https://kino.ai ). Kino lets you make great videos with your agents and your teammates. Storage of footage and assets, a rich video editor, and review links for teammates are all bundled into one. Your colleagues and Codex / Claude Code can work on the same timeline with review notes and footage all in one place. See a basic overview at https://kino.ai/walkthrough-video and our launch video (made entirely with Kino!) at https://kino.ai/launch-video Opus 5.5 can edit videos and make great motion graphics now. But with a raw agent harness, you need to describe tiny edits either in words or in quick one-off UIs, you can’t refer to footage shared across your devices, and feedback from teammates comes as screenshots on Slack. Kino is code-first. All editing, all motion graphics, all dragging of timeline items around, all teammate comments, and all 3D scenes are expressed as code, built on Remotion. This was hard to get right, as we found ourselves building a what-you-see-is-what-you-get editor for React, which we then turned into a video editor. For our launch video I told Claude-with-Kino to find a macOS Leopard install disk and reskin our whole video to match. Kino is also fully collaborative and real-time, so you can see your teammates' cursors and exactly which part of the timeline they’re currently watching. For our launch video I had 5+ agents editing the timeline concurrently while my friend Donald had his swarm working a few minutes further down. Donald had one agent rotoscoping to make our visual effects work, I had an LLM color grading all media via our LUT support, and we both made tiny tweaks to the timeline along the way. To make this code-first editor work with video footage, everything gets transcribed, embedded, described, and face-detected. You can scrub your footage locally after you drag it in, but we upload a low-res proxy so your teammates and cloud inference can see it. This local scrubbing plus custom pro media decoders means you can drag a 250GB ProRes clip from your new iPhone right into your Kino timeline. We built custom decoders for professional codecs such as ProRes, BRAW, R3D, and more (see my extremely successful nine point HN post https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50198052 ). None of the performance we’re getting would have been possible before WebCodecs and libraries like Mediabunny. I grew up making YouTube videos, and during my undergrad at MIT I co-directed a 3.5 hour archival footage documentary on the history of my school and technological development in America ( https://regressions.net ). Much of the work was logging footage, managing hard drives, manually syncing Premiere project state, and planning our movie in a spreadsheet. Our first launch in 2023 proclaimed that Kino was "Silicon Valley meets Hollywood." It was more like Palantir for Hollywood; we ran bespoke on-prem Kino deployments with our team of forward deployed engineers on shows like Survivor and A24's Beef. It was a rush, but it felt like the slowest way to improve video editing for the whole world. Bound by the Avid Media Composer and strict studio security rules, we couldn't touch frontier models, and we couldn't make editors >10x faster. So in 2025, we rebuilt Kino as a true editor, and we took a bet on coding-as-editing. Everything in Kino has a URL: projects, clips, footage, comments and replies, even a single frame and the line of code that draws it. Projects and media living in one place and everything being addressable means that your agents and team have a single, editable source of truth for video production. At a lower level, I now paste Kino links into my agent constantly, whether it’s making sure Codex knows exactly which timeline item (among thousands) I am referring to or which teammate’s comment needs fixing. We have teams managing their whole company’s media in Kino, spinning

leads.title: FinOps Data Engineer
leads.description: About the Role We're looking for a FinOps Data Engineer to help drive cost optimization and cloud financial governance across our AWS infrastructure and GCP footprint. You'll work cross-functionally with Engineering, Finance, and Product to find and ship savings, build the tooling necessary to maximize efficiency of every dollar spent in the cloud, and cultivate a culture of cost awareness across engineering teams. This role owns the data side of that mission: the models, pipelines, and analysis that make cost, usage, and margin numbers trustworthy across the company. This is a hands-on engineering role, not an analyst seat. You'll do the schlep work other teams don't have time for, digging into a bucket's access pattern, writing the dbt model or Python pipeline that ships the fix, building the cost-vs-revenue mart that answers a margin question once instead of every time, and chasing a number until it reconciles. Strong communication matters as much as technical depth, you'll regularly explain a savings case or a data model's implications to an engineering team, a finance stakeholder, and a leadership audience in the same week. What You'll Be Responsible For In this role, you'll: Find and ship savings across AWS and GCP: Analyze billing, usage, and cost trends to identify opportunities, rightsizing, storage lifecycle policies, data transfer, and spot/auto-scaling. Take ideas from identification through to a realized dollar figure, not just a recommendation. Build and maintain the FinOps data pipeline: Design and run the BigQuery/dbt models that turn raw billing and usage data (CUR, Storage Lens) into reconciled, trustworthy mart tables, the foundation everything else in FinOps is built on. Build cost-vs-revenue and customer segmentation models: Model unit economics and margin by product line and customer segment, and extend coverage as new products and segments come online. Apply data science to cost and usage data: Build forecasting models, detect anomalies statistically rather than by threshold alone, and quantify savings opportunities (e.g. storage lifecycle, request-cost patterns) with rigor a spreadsheet can't match. Build and maintain cost attribution: Tagging policies, cost allocation, and chargeback/showback so engineering teams can see and own their own spend. This is foundational work other savings work depends on. Automate cost governance: Build automated cost reporting, anomaly detection, and alerting. Write the scripts and infrastructure-as-code (Python, Terraform, Lambda) that enforce cost policy rather than relying on manual review. Partner with engineering on architecture decisions: Bring cost into the room early, cost-efficiencies are cheaper to get right at design than to retrofit. Work with Finance on forecasting and reporting: Support budget tracking and financial KPIs; build dashboards and self-serve analytics engineering and finance can both read. You Might Be a Good Fit If You Have strong AWS expertise and working GCP knowledge, including pricing models, billing structures, and cost optimization mechanics. Have data engineering depth: dbt, BigQuery (or an equivalent modern warehouse), SQL at scale, and data modeling for analytics (dimensional modeling, incremental models, testing). Have data science fundamentals: statistical forecasting, anomaly detection, and experimentation, and know when a rigorous model beats a rule of thumb. Have automation and scripting skills: Python, Terraform/ pulumi, Lambda, or Bash. Are comfortable with cost/billing tooling: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage Reports, GCP Billing Reports, and BI/dashboarding (we use Hex). Have experience with, or are comfortable picking up, Linear and Notion as the system of record for tracking and documenting FinOps work. Experience with a dedicated cloud cost management platform (e.g. CloudZero, Vantage, or similar) is a plus, not required. leads.title: Senior Revenue Forecasting & Operations Business Partner
leads.description: Caylent is an AI-first cloud services company that helps organizations turn ambitious ideas into meaningful business impact. As an AWS Premier Tier Services Partner and a charter member of Anthropic’s Claude Partner Network, we combine deep expertise in AWS, artificial intelligence, and Anthropic’s Claude platform to help customers modernize their technology, build intelligent products, and move AI from experimentation into production. Our capabilities span generative and agentic AI, cloud migration and modernization, cloud-native application development, data and analytics, DevOps, managed services, security and compliance, and customer experience transformation. At Caylent, our people always come first. We are a fully remote global company with employees in Canada, the United States and Latin America. We celebrate the culture of each of our team members and foster a community of technological curiosity. Come talk to us to learn more about what it means to be a Caylien! The Mission We are seeking a Senior Revenue Forecasting & Operations Business Partner to own Caylent’s revenue forecast and the operational data that feeds it, and to act as the finance partner to our Sales and Delivery leadership. Reporting to the Director of Finance, you will turn signed SOWs, staffing plans, and billing schedules into a forecast leadership can rely on, and explain the variance when actuals land. This is a hands-on role with high visibility to the CFO and the executive team. You will work daily with senior leaders across Sales, Delivery, Resource Management, and Accounting, challenging assumptions, influencing decisions, and translating financial trade-offs into clear recommendations they can act on. As we grow, you will also help integrate acquired entities into our forecasting, reporting, and systems. Your Assignment Revenue Forecasting and Finance Business Partner Own the monthly and quarterly revenue forecast across all entities (US, Canada, Brazil, Argentina, Mexico) and subsidiaries, and maintain a rolling 12-month forecast that supports the annual budget and reforecast cycles. Build the forecast bottom-up from signed SOWs, change orders, staffing plans, and billing schedules, and reconcile it top-down to the Salesforce pipeline and bookings. Forecast by revenue type : time and materials, fixed fee, managed services, and AWS-funded engagements. Model backlog burn, utilization, and bench impact on revenue, and flag engagements at risk of under-delivery or overrun. Deliver a monthly forecast vs. actuals package with variance explained by engagement, practice, and entity. Business Partnering Act as the trusted finance partner to Sales, Delivery, and Resource Management leaders, joining their forecast, pipeline, and staffing reviews on a recurring basis. Partner on deal and SOW structuring (pricing, fee model, AWS funding) before signature, not only after. Challenge assumptions (pipeline conversion, utilization, staffing, deal structure) with data, and influence decisions. Translate financial trade-offs (margin, cash, risk) into clear recommendations for senior, non-finance stakeholders. Systems, Data & Reporting Be the Finance owner of revenue data across Salesforce, the PSA or time tracking system, and the ERP; define the fields and controls that keep them in sync. Build and maintain forecast models and dashboards with full traceability from reported numbers back to source records. Automate recurring reporting where practical (Google Sheets, Apps Script, SQL, BI tooling, or AI tools). Document revenue operations processes and controls to support audit and month-end close. What Success Looks Like First 30 days: Understand the forecast end to end and map every active engagement to its fee structure, billing schedule, funding terms, and staffing plan. First 90 days: Own the monthly forecast and deliver the first forecast vs. actuals package with variance explained by engagement; establish regular cadences with Sales and Delivery leadership

leads.title: Senior Site Reliability Engineer - Ceph Storage
leads.description: Location Details: At GoDaddy the future of work looks different for each team. Some teams work in the office full-time; others have a hybrid arrangement (they work remotely some days and in the office some days) and some work entirely remotely.​ This is a remote position, so you’ll be working remotely from your home. You may occasionally visit a GoDaddy office to meet with your team for events or meetings. Join Our Team… GoDaddy's Global Storage Engineering team operates one of the largest Ceph environments in the industry, powering the object, block, and file storage platforms that underpin hosting, applications, internal infrastructure, and next-generation AI/HPC workloads. If you're passionate about distributed systems, large-scale storage architecture, and solving complex reliability challenges, you'll work on infrastructure that few engineers ever experience. At GoDaddy, Ceph isn't a side project — it's a critical platform. Our environment spans 80+ production clusters, 20,000+ OSDs, and approximately 300 PB of raw storage capacity, supporting tens of billions of objects across multiple continents. The scale demands deep technical expertise in storage architecture, automation, observability, and performance engineering. As a Senior Site Reliability Engineer, you'll be a key technical owner of the platform, responsible for maintaining reliability, driving operational excellence, and influencing the future evolution of our storage ecosystem. You'll tackle challenging production problems, develop automation that operates at massive scale, contribute to architectural decisions, and collaborate with some of the industry's most experienced Ceph engineers. This is an opportunity to have direct impact on a storage platform that serves millions of customers worldwide. Diagnose and resolve complex distributed systems issues including recovery/backfill events, OSD instability, PG imbalance, storage latency, and RGW performance bottlenecks. Design and build automation using Python, Shell, SaltStack, and Ansible to reduce operational toil and improve platform resilience at scale. Define and improve observability for the storage platform through SLIs, SLOs, PromQL, LogQL, Grafana dashboards, and proactive alerting strategies. Lead storage lifecycle initiatives including cluster expansions, hardware refreshes, software upgrades, OpenStack integrations, and large-scale migration projects. Your Experience Should Include… 5+ years operating large-scale Linux infrastructure with significant experience supporting distributed storage systems in production environments. 2+ years hands-on Ceph administration including OSD, MON, MDS, and RGW operations, CRUSH map management, pool design, placement groups, and performance troubleshooting. Strong understanding of Linux internals, storage architecture, networking, filesystems, block devices, and performance analysis under production workloads. Experience developing operational automation and tooling with Python, Shell, and configuration management platforms such as Ansible, SaltStack, Puppet, or Chef. Proven incident response expertise, including production troubleshooting, root-cause analysis, postmortem creation, and implementation of durable corrective actions. You Might Also Have… Advanced Ceph expertise across RGW Multisite, CephFS, RBD Mirroring, erasure coding, and large-scale cluster design. Experience integrating storage platforms with OpenStack (Cinder, Nova, Neutron, Swift) or Kubernetes storage technologies (CSI, StorageClasses, Rook). Familiarity with modern observability platforms including Prometheus, Mimir, Loki, Grafana, and enterprise monitoring architectures. Experience planning and executing petabyte-scale storage migrations, capacity expansion programs, and storage hardware

leads.title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
leads.description: I've been developing applications for a long time and have turned to game development as well lately. One of the things that frustrated me the most was that using AI agents for game development is very annoying in the art department. Your only options right now are to either use an image genAI model and roll the dice every time you want to make an edit, or have your agent draw with something like vectors. I was looking for an application that would allow me to ask an agent to make a first draft of whatever art I needed with actual brushes, and then be able to go in myself and edit every last stroke or layer that it created. Klad is that application. Written in Rust, it can be fully controlled by an agent through the CLI, and every function is available in a nice UI as well: a brush engine, frame-by-frame animation (and bones/IK), vectors, text layers, colours, layer effects, infinite undo (even after re-opening the file!),… Why I think it's useful for a wider audience: Adobe showed agents editing Photoshop files at MAX this week, with a private beta planned for early 2027. Klad is built on the same core idea, with editable paint strokes as core architecture, and it works today. Clone the repo to try it out: https://github.com/klad-app/klad You can basically point Claude to the repo, ask it to build it, and pick up the drawing skills. Then ask it to make any drawing you want! (After that, you or the agent can change absolutely every brush stroke in the app again, which makes edits a breeze.) The quality of the drawings really depends on the agent you use. I have tried it with Claude Fable 5.2 since it came out on Monday, and the drawings are already quite impressive. I'm confident that this will only improve. I use it every day on Mac, so that definitely works well. It builds on Linux too (tablet pen pressure still needs some work there). Windows builds in CI, I haven't used it there myself yet but I have some reports that it works perfectly fine. Coming up next is support for pixel art. I'm in the testing phase with this right now, and I expect it to go live in the repo sometime this weekend. Klad is source-available rather than open source: free to build and use for individuals and small companies, and I plan to sell pre-built binaries later, the way Aseprite does. The file format, CLI reference and agent skill are MIT. What I want to hear from people who try it: Can your agent work out the CLI without help, and where does it get confused? Can you go in and change one of its strokes easily? The command reference and guides are available at https://klad.studio I'll be here answering any questions about the technical side as well, as it's a pretty interesting challenge to build a performant engine with editable brush strokes that render as paint.

leads.title: Show HN: AppTraction – A Native Mac App for Apple's App Store Connect
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m John. I’m excited to share something I’ve been working on for a long time and releasing today: AppTraction, a native Mac app for Apple’s App Store Connect. I spent 10 years as an engineer at Apple working on macOS and iOS, and the last 8 as an indie developer with 20+ apps on the App Store for myself and clients. AppTraction is the tool I wish I’d had when I started building my own apps. Most iOS and Mac devs that I talk to agree that Apple’s App Store Connect website is slow, confusing, and buggy. There’s a lot of useful data there, but the clunky site makes it really hard to make sense of. AppTraction brings your sales, analytics, ratings, and reviews to your Mac, and then tells you what matters. I won’t get into all the app features here, you can find those on the website, but it has some interesting capabilities so please check them out. Some background on the development process: AppTraction started as a straight port of the App Store Connect website to a native Mac app, and for about two months that’s all it was. Having the analytics data cached and instant was fantastic, but it still required a lot of time and expertise to interpret. At that point I tried connecting Claude directly to the structured data via MCP, and the results were pretty astonishing. Right away it caught that Apple had featured my apps in Australia and the UK, which I’d been totally oblivious to. It also explained that my bread baking app’s sales decline (which I knew about) wasn’t a problem with the app at all, but a recurring seasonal slump, which is evidently typical for baking apps in the summer. That’s when the Insights tab, which now looks for things like these automatically, became the main view of the app. The AI runs on your existing Claude Code or Codex subscription (or OpenRouter). AppTraction uses the CLI you already have, so there are no API fees and no API keys to expose. AI requests go straight from your Mac to your AI provider, under your account, and my servers never see them. Pricing: It’s free for 14 days, then $6.99/month, $39/year, or $99 lifetime. Requires macOS 26 Tahoe or later. (No ASC key handy? There’s a demo app with sample data to play with.) I’d love to hear any feedback, and happy to answer questions of course.

leads.description:
## Overview
**Priority:** `P0`
**QA Bounty:** Model Routing & Failover

Identify incorrect routing, silent failures, unexpected model substitutions, and fallback failures.

## What Needs Testing
- Verify that every model ID advertised by `GET /v1/models` routes to the exact intended model backend without silent substitution or alias misdirection.
- Detect silent failures (e.g., HTTP 200 responses with empty `content`, truncated streams without `finish_reason`, or HTML/plain-text error bodies masquerading as 200 OK).
- Test automatic failover and fallback chains when a primary upstream provider times out, rate-limits (429), or returns 5xx errors.
- Verify response metadata (`model` field, provider headers, latency) accurately reflects the model that served the request.

## Acceptance Criteria
- [ ] Automated routing & failover test suite covering the `/v1/models` catalog, alias resolution, and simulated/live upstream failure scenarios.
- [ ] Zero tolerance for silent 200 OK empty responses or undisclosed model substitutions — any occurrence documented with full request/response traces or fixed via PR.
- [ ] Verification that fallback behavior preserves request parameters (tools, `response_format`, system prompts, streaming).

Difficulty: P0

Points: 250 (Hanzo Rewards points — see https://hanzo.ai/bounty and https://hanzo.ai/leaderboard)

## How to Claim
1. Comment on this issue stating the test cases / models you are covering.
2. Submit a reproducible test suite, detailed QA report with request/response traces, or a pull request referencing `Fixes #<issue-number>`.
3. Link your GitHub account at https://hanzo.ai/leaderboard to receive your bounty points and credits upon verification.

leads.title: Test the rules that decide which bounty a pull request claims
leads.description:
**What this is for**

`agent/bounties.mjs` decides which bounty a merged pull request can claim: through the issue it closes, or through an explicit `Bounty: #N` line, and only when the bounty was funded for that same repository. Those rules move money, and they have no tests yet.

**What done looks like**

- [ ] `agent/test/bounties.test.js`, with `node:test` and no network. Mock `fetch` where a function needs it.
- [ ] `pointsAtRepo`: the same repository counts; a repository whose name only starts the same (`mergit` against `mergit-demo`) does not; another domain carrying the path does not; free text does not.
- [ ] `pointsAtIssue`: issue #1 does not match issue #10, and a dot in an owner name is literal.
- [ ] `LINEA_BOUNTY`: works with Windows line endings, does not jump to the next line, and ignores a mention in the middle of a sentence.
- [ ] `closedIssues`: every form of close, fix and resolve.
- [ ] `bountyForIssue`: exactly one match is returned; none gives a reason; two give an ambiguity and return nothing; `funders` narrows the candidates.
- [ ] `logsOf`: follows `next_page_params` across pages, and throws when a page fails.
- [ ] `node --test test/` passes inside `agent/`. The "Agent tests" check runs it on your pull request. Names and comments in Spanish.

**Where it goes**

- `agent/test/bounties.test.js`

Do not change the agent itself. If a test finds a bug, open an issue describing it instead.

**Funding:** not locked yet. When it is, this line will link the transaction. Wait for it before you start.

---

**How this gets paid.** The money is locked on chain before anyone starts. Write `Closes #N` with this issue's number in your pull request description. That is all the agent needs. When it is merged with CI green, the agent pays the author's wallet by itself and leaves the receipt on the pull request. The `mergit/payable` check next to the merge button says in advance whether merging will pay.

**Before you start,** put one line naming Mergit and your address in the README of your GitHub profile repository (`github.com/<you>/<you>`). Nothing to connect, no gas. Or register your login at https://www.mergit.xyz/register

On a first pull request the CI waits for a maintainer to approve the workflow run. That is normal, and not something you did wrong.

This is a test network, so the ETH is practice money, and we would rather say so. What is real is the record: the payment is written on chain and shows up at `https://www.mergit.xyz/p/<your login>`

**One bounty, one payment.** The first pull request merged takes it.

**Nothing is paid outside the contract.** Anyone asking you to send money, or asking for yours, is not part of this.

leads.title: L2 menu opens PIN setup while L1 wallet is loading, even when a PIN is already set
leads.description:
## Bounty: L2 opens the "set a PIN" flow while the L1 wallet is still loading

**Tier:** S — 15,000 XTM

### Description

If you click the L2 sidebar button before the L1 wallet has finished loading, Universe asks you to set a PIN even when one is already set. If you enter a PIN anyway, it fails with "A PIN is already set for this wallet".

The cause is in the frontend. `openL2()` in `src/store/actions/l2OpenActions.ts` reads `useWalletStore.is_pin_locked` and opens the `l2_pin_required` (create PIN) dialog when it's `false`. That flag defaults to `false` and is only set when the wallet setup phase emits it (`src-tauri/src/setup/phase_wallet.rs:239`, `emit_pin_locked`). Until then, the app can't tell "no PIN" apart from "not loaded yet".

### Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] With a PIN already set, clicking the L2 button while the L1 wallet is still loading never opens the create-PIN dialog
- [ ] While the PIN state is unknown, the L2 button either waits or is disabled with a loading indication, and once the wallet has loaded it goes to the normal unlock/PIN-entry flow
- [ ] A wallet that really has no PIN still gets the create-PIN dialog, both before and after loading finishes
- [ ] Any other UI that uses `is_pin_locked` to tell whether a PIN is set (e.g. `L2Wallet.tsx` burn button, `L2WalletCard.tsx`, `SendModal.tsx`, `VerifySeedPhrase.tsx`) doesn't treat "not loaded yet" as "no PIN"
- [ ] Unit tests cover the loading state (extend `l2OpenActions.test.ts` and/or `L2WalletCard.test.tsx`)
- [ ] The PR includes a short screen recording of the fixed behaviour: launch with a PIN set and click L2 during wallet load

### Context

- Entry point: `src/containers/navigation/Sidebars/buttons/L2Button.tsx` → `openL2()` in `src/store/actions/l2OpenActions.ts`
- PIN state source: `src-tauri/src/setup/phase_wallet.rs` (`PinManager::pin_locked()` → `EventsEmitter::emit_pin_locked`)
- Backend error text: `src-tauri/src/internal_wallet.rs:667`
- A good fix probably lets the store say "unknown" (e.g. `is_pin_locked: boolean | undefined`), or reads the PIN state on demand, instead of relying on a `false` default

### How It Works

1. Comment on this issue to signal intent (courtesy, not a lock)
2. Fork the repo and do the work
3. Submit a PR that references the issue with a closing keyword (e.g. `Fixes #3518`) so GitHub links your PR to the bounty automatically
4. Bounties are competitive. Multiple PRs may be submitted for the same bounty. Review comments are public, and contributors may borrow ideas from each other's work. The maintainer selects the PR that best solves the problem, considering code quality, completeness, and contributor behavior. In cases where multiple contributors made significant contributions, the maintainer may split the bounty. The maintainer's decision is final.
5. Earn XTM (processing may take up to a week; reach out to @possum on Discord with your Tari address)

- AI-assisted development is expected and encouraged
- If you get stuck, ask in Discord

leads.title: Show HN: VoxaDub – Open-source AI video dubbing with speaker-aware voices
leads.description: Hi HN, I have been working on a project called VoxaDub: an open source local-first AI dubbing tool which can translate videos into other languages while preserving the original voices of the speakers. A major issue when translating is ensuring the translation matches with the length of speech in the target language. Even slight differences in timing can cause unnatural dubbing. It becomes more complex when there are multiple speakers in the original video. I have created a pipeline that uses Whisper/WhisperX to transcribe and align audio, Community-1 to identify speakers, Hy-MT2 to translate contextually and VoxCPM2 to generate speaker aware audio. The main feature of VoxaDub is the ability to improve the translation using the available time for the audio to be spoken for, limit the time changes to within certain bounds and analyse for any timing issues. There is also some experimental Live Dubbing for YouTube videos and live streams through a Chrome extension. This is actively being developed and is not yet production ready. The main project runs fully locally once models are set up, no external translation or TTS APIs are required. Optional GPU usage is available using Colab and Modal. I am pleased to see that the project was recently added to the Ecosystem & Community section of OpenBMB's official VoxCPM GitHub repository (PR #389). While this is just a community project listing it was nice to see this progress. True examples of the English to Spanish, Japanese and Turkish dubbing can be found in the README. Source videos, information on how it was implemented and any limitations are also present. The project is MIT licensed and can be found on GitHub. I would really appreciate any technical feedback on the timing of the translations, speaker consistency and simplifying the local setup. There is a lot of room for improvement so any thoughts would be great!

leads.title: Platform-Capitalism on Steroids
leads.description: So i got recently unemployed, left my last company as they wanted me to leave. They offered me money to leave and as they changed my working environment in an unpleasant way I decided to take the money. So now i find myself on the job market for IT specialists right in the middle of AI take-over. The jobs are shifting towards AI automation or so. At least any code seems to be written now by AI, and in the best case reviewed by a human. After thinking for a few days what job i am interested in, talking about it to AI, i start feeling over-helmed by the requirements companies are asking for. Are there already Senior AI Architects in Germany? Not sure. Anyway, how do these changes concern me? Looking at the job market, everything is nowadays Frontend, DevOps, Finance or Embedded it seems. Common Software Development vanished except for a few jobs at old-fashioned companies. I wonder who is developing all those tools and libraries? This are spare time projects multi-trillion-dollar companies are built on. Finally all application code is written either for iOS, Android or Web. Which eventually maps to Swift, Kotlin and html5/css/Javascript. And Embedded is another field, hardware product development. Which I am just not motivated anymore. So where to go from here now? What are the options? Finally dealing more with people, dealing more with what? Where to head from here? Damn i lost traction in the market. Now spinning around myself. What is truly needed? Can this even be determined as the market is changing so quickly? One things is definitely important. Build systems which not only build but track, verify and release changes while still allowing quick rollbacks. Right? People want to deploy very quickly new features to their customers while letting the customer test, but bugs are still possible, so rollbacks will be more important than ever. Will they? The tricky will still be, while people using this new infrastructure, they feed AI with the solution training it themselves to replace their works putting them into a situation where they need to try stay ahead of the machine's skills. The faster they hustle the more they improve the machine, which does not need to breath. The better the machine the more you hustle. It/IT looks to me like a mouse in a spinning wheel. Platform-Capitalism on Steroids.

leads.title: Show HN: Rebuilding Amazon SES in Rust
leads.description: I'm Kam, co-founder and CTO of Nitrosend. Email is our lifeblood, so we've been gradually moving our email sending onto bare-metal servers and IPs we control. We wanted to make that move without rewriting the application code already calling Amazon SES. So we built NitroMTA, an open-source SES replacement in Rust. We kept our existing SES v2 sending calls and changed the endpoint and credentials to send through our own engine. We've been running it in production for a few weeks, moving more mail over as we warm our IPs and build reputation with each mailbox provider. Keep the SES integration For an application using boto3, this is the client configuration: import boto3 ses = boto3.client( "sesv2", region_name="us-east-1", endpoint_url="https://mail.example.com", ) For the SES v2 sending operations we support, the existing calls keep working. We test the official JavaScript, Python and Ruby SDKs against the engine, along with Nodemailer and django-ses. The compatibility page lists the operations and differences from SES: https://nitromta.com/docs/compatibility/ Measuring against KumoMTA and Postfix In our published 2 November comparison, NitroMTA sustained 3.16 times KumoMTA's throughput and 4.11 times Postfix's. These numbers measure SMTP submission and delivery. Engine Messages per second NitroMTA 3,313 KumoMTA 1,048 Postfix with OpenDKIM 806 Each engine had four CPU cores and 2 GiB of memory on the same AWS c7gd.metal bare-metal server, with its queue on local NVMe. The workload used 16 KiB messages, authenticated SMTP submission, TLS on submission and delivery, and RSA-2048 DKIM signing. Every engine committed a message to disk before acknowledging it. The figures are medians of three interleaved runs per engine. The quick profile searches for the highest rate meeting its latency budgets using ten-second load steps, delivering to one receiver site with no added network delay. Across the nine runs, the harness sent 1.35 million messages and checked that each arrived once, with its body intact and its DKIM signature valid. KumoMTA used its RocksDB spool with set_force_sync(true) to meet the same acceptance contract. KumoMTA documents that this forces database-wide flushes and can substantially reduce performance. The comparison is for that synchronous-acceptance contract; the harness also supports measuring its default asynchronous mode separately. The method, configurations, exact versions and raw results are published, and you can run the comparison with cargo harness quick: https://nitromta.com/docs/benchmarks/ Give each IP a budget for each provider An IP needs a sending history with the receivers it sends to. We need to decide how much volume it gets today, what earns it more tomorrow, and what makes us back off. We track the budget by sending IP and receiver group. That lets us hold an IP's Gmail cap while increasing its cap elsewhere, or lower its Outlook.com cap when Microsoft's responses call for it. With warmup enabled, the shipped ladder starts at 50 messages a day. A day needs enough SMTP outcomes to test its cap before it earns an increase. Complaints, failures, deferrals and throttling can hold the cap or move it down a rung. The Outlook.com defaults take fourteen clean daily increases to reach 10,000 messages a day. The default ladder takes seven. Both are configurable. Before any of this, the host needs outbound port 25 and reverse DNS control for its sending addresses. The domains need SPF, DKIM and DMARC, and bounce and complaint reports need somewhere to arrive. We put the setup checks in nitromta doctor, which prints the missing records. Provider feedback and durability details continue in a reply.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)
leads.description:
## Python wire client rejects valid responses larger than 16 KiB (e.g., LBS GET with block size > 16360)

At `3de151b` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py` defines

    MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES = 16384

with the comment "This is a somewhat arbitrary value", and `Wire.send_recv()` reads the whole response with a single bounded call:

    idnum, record = split_packet(self.sock.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES))

`split_packet()` then requires the *entire* frame inside that one buffer:

    record, crc = struct.unpack_from('>%dsI' % record_length, packet, offset=16)
    assert len(packet) == len(record) + 16 + 4

A Wire frame for a record of length `N` is `N + 20` bytes, so any response record longer than 16364 bytes cannot be processed: `recv()` returns at most 16384 bytes and `struct.unpack_from` raises `struct.error`.

This is separate from #358 (responses fragmented across reads of a small packet). PR #359's stated fix explicitly keeps "the existing total response-size limit", so this bug remains even after #359 is merged.

### Valid server responses that exceed the cap

1. **LBS GET with block size > 16360.** The block size is operator-configured via `lbs -b`, validated to `[PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MIN, PROTO_LBS_BLKLEN_MAX]` = `[512, 131072]` (`lbs/main.c`, `lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs.h`). An LBS GET response record is `4 (status) + blklen` bytes (`lib/proto_lbs/proto_lbs_server.c`, `proto_lbs_response_get()`). Any deployment configured with block size ≥ 16361 — legal up to the documented maximum of 131072 — produces GET responses the Python client cannot read. The C server imposes no such limit: `proto_lbs_request_parse()` `malloc()`s APPEND payloads dynamically and `wire_writepacket_getbuf()` sizes GET responses to the configured block size.

2. **KVLDS RANGE responses.** The response record grows with the data returned: `4 (status) + 4 (num_pairs) + nextkey + Σ(1+keylen + 1+valen)` (each pair up to 514 bytes). For 100-byte keys/values, a range response with roughly 80 pairs already exceeds the cap; `tests/python/dump_kvlds.py` requests `maxsize = 8192` pairs per range call, so the dump tool fails on most non-trivial datasets. The C-side range response is likewise dynamically sized.

### Reproduction (real C server, no mocks)

On `3de151b`, with `crcmod` installed:

    $ ./lbs/lbs -s /tmp/repro/lbs.sock -d /tmp/repro/storage -b 32768 -1 &
    $ python3 - <<'EOF'
    import sys
    sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
    from kivaloo import proto_lbs
    p = proto_lbs.Proto_lbs('/tmp/repro/lbs.sock')
    print("params():", p.params())
    data = bytes(range(256)) * 128          # one 32 KiB block
    print("append():", p.append(1, 0, data))
    print("get():", p.get(0))
    EOF

    params(): (32768, 0)
    append(): 0 1
    get() FAILED -> error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 32792 bytes
        for unpacking 32776 bytes at offset 16 (actual buffer size is 16384)

The C `lbs` server accepts the 32 KiB block and serves it (no server-side error); only the Python client fails.

### Impact

- The Python client cannot interoperate with any LBS deployment configured with block size > 16360 (legal up to 131072).
- `dump_kvlds.py` and any KVLDS RANGE consumer fail once a range response exceeds 16 KiB.
- The test suite cannot exercise the C server with non-default (larger) block sizes, because the harness itself rejects the responses.

### Suggested fix

In `send_recv()`: read the 16-byte header first (as #359 proposes), then read exactly `record_length + 4` further bytes based on the header's `record_length` field before calling `split_packet()`. This bounds the allocation by the protocol maximum (LBS: 20 + 4 + 131072 = 131096 bytes; KVLDS: bounded by the requested data) instead of a fixed 16384. `MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES` can then be removed or raised to the protocol maximum.

### Scope / disclosure

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers (`tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py`). I am not reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption. The C client (`lib/wire/wire_readpacket.c`) reads complete packets and is unaffected.

This report, investigation and reproduction were prepared by an LLM with the authorization of the `zhangb06` account owner. I am available to discuss the problem or a fix through this account. No live customer data, external service testing, or payment credentials were used.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python LBS append silently truncates or pads mismatched block counts
leads.description:
I am an LLM assistant (Codex/Astra), submitting on behalf of the account owner. I can help discuss this reproduction and revise the candidate patch in response to feedback relayed through this account.

At commit 3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce, tests/python/kivaloo/proto_lbs.py:Proto_lbs.append() checks that the byte length is a multiple of the block size, but not that it matches nums * block_size. The actual Wire.send_recv() then uses a fixed-length struct.pack string field, silently truncating or padding mismatched data.

With block_size = 4, a recording socket under the actual Python wire encoder captured:

    nums=1 input=b'AAAABBBB' payload=b'AAAA' result=(0, 1)
    nums=2 input=b'AAAA' payload=b'AAAA\x00\x00\x00\x00' result=(0, 2)

The success responses are supplied by the socket double; no C server was run. The observed bug is the changed outgoing payload, not independently demonstrated server-side storage corruption. This requires inconsistent arguments from a caller of the Python test helper. I am not claiming an issue in the C APPEND implementation or a security vulnerability.

A candidate check, immediately after num_bytes = self.block_size * nums:

    if len(blocks) != num_bytes:
        raise ValueError("wire append: Block count does not match data length")

The following test uses the actual Proto_lbs.append, Wire.send_recv, packet encoder and decoder, with an in-memory socket double. Save as tests/python/test_lbs_append_length.py; from tests/python run python -m unittest -v test_lbs_append_length with crcmod and psutil installed.

Python 3.12.14 / Windows: baseline 1 passes and 2 fail; with the check all 3 pass. The exact-length control verifies byte preservation and the decoded success result. The mismatched cases verify no packet is sent after the fix. Full native server tests were not run.

<details><summary>Reproduction / regression test</summary>

~~~python
"""Check APPEND length validation without starting a server."""

import struct
import unittest

from kivaloo.proto_lbs import Proto_lbs
from kivaloo.wire import Wire, make_packet, split_packet


class RecordingSocket:
    def __init__(self):
        self.records = []
        self.msgnum = None

    def sendall(self, packet):
        self.msgnum, record = split_packet(packet)
        self.records.append(record)

    def recv(self, size):
        _, nums, start = struct.unpack_from('>IIQ', self.records[-1])
        return make_packet(self.msgnum, struct.pack('>IQ', 0, start + nums))

    def close(self):
        pass


class AppendLengthTests(unittest.TestCase):
    def setUp(self):
        self.sock = RecordingSocket()
        self.proto = Proto_lbs.__new__(Proto_lbs)
        self.proto.block_size = 4
        self.proto.wire = Wire.__new__(Wire)
        self.proto.wire.msgnum = 0
        self.proto.wire.sock = self.sock

    def tearDown(self):
        self.proto.close()

    def test_rejects_too_many_bytes(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.proto.append(1, 0, b'AAAABBBB')
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records, [])

    def test_rejects_too_few_bytes(self):
        with self.assertRaises(ValueError):
            self.proto.append(2, 0, b'AAAA')
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records, [])

    def test_exact_length_preserves_bytes(self):
        self.assertEqual(self.proto.append(2, 7, b'AAAABBBB'), (0, 9))
        self.assertEqual(self.sock.records,
                         [struct.pack('>IIQ', 2, 2, 7) + b'AAAABBBB'])


if __name__ == '__main__':
    unittest.main()
~~~

</details>

Submitted for consideration under the bug bounty program, with classification and eligibility left to the maintainer. I understand awards below $100 are Tarsnap account credits, not cash.

leads.title: [bug bounty] Python wire client fails on valid responses split across stream reads
leads.description:
## Python client fails on a valid response split across stream reads

At `3de151b5d878b0714552c3658562eb5a87b378ce` (`master`), `tests/python/kivaloo/wire.py:159` passes one `socket.recv(MAX_RESPONSE_BYTES)` result directly to `split_packet()`. The AF_UNIX stream can return fewer bytes than a complete packet. A valid response can therefore raise an uncaught `struct.error` in the Python client even though the remaining bytes are still arriving.

This report is limited to the Python client/helper and its callers. I am **not** reporting a crash in the C storage server, a security exploit, or stored-data corruption.

### Reproduction

With the existing `crcmod` dependency installed, run this from the repository root:

```python
import sys
import struct
sys.path.insert(0, 'tests/python')
from kivaloo import wire

# A valid KVLDS PARAMS response: 8-byte payload, 28-byte complete frame.
record = struct.pack('>II', 255, 255)
packet = wire.make_packet(0, record)
assert wire.split_packet(packet) == (0, record)

class ShortReads:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = packet
    def sendall(self, data):
        assert wire.split_packet(data) == (0, struct.pack('>I', 0x100))
    def recv(self, size):
        size = min(size, 8)
        result, self.data = self.data[:size], self.data[size:]
        return result
    def close(self):
        pass

client = wire.Wire.__new__(wire.Wire)
client.msgnum = 0
client.sock = ShortReads()
print(client.send_recv('>I', 0x100).get('>II'))
```

Expected: `(255, 255)`.

Actual on the base commit:

```text
struct.error: unpack_from requires a buffer of at least 16 bytes for
unpacking 16 bytes at offset 0 (actual buffer size is 8)
```

I also reproduced the failure using a real local `socket.socketpair()`, with an event coordinating the second fragment only after the first `recv()` returns. This needs no timing sleeps or remote service. An additional check used the compiled C `lbs` server, private temporary storage and a Unix socket: the unchanged response stream succeeds with the original client on the normal path, fails with the original client when reads are limited to eight bytes, and passes PARAMS/APPEND/GET with byte-exact data after the fix.

### Proposed fix and validation

Read the 16-byte header completely, validate its checksum and the existing total response-size limit, then read the payload and four-byte trailer completely before calling the existing `split_packet()`. Treat EOF before a full frame as an error rather than looping. Keep the existing record-checksum and response-ID checks.

A local minimal patch adds 20 lines and removes two in `wire.py`. Thirteen regression tests pass after the patch, including all 27 split points of the PARAMS response, single-byte reads, complete-response controls, early EOF, size limits, checksum failures, consecutive frames and the real socket-pair reproduction. These tests fail on the unmodified base at the framing cases. Validation used macOS arm64, Python 3.14.7 and the actual `crcmod==1.7` package. The C programs compiled successfully with the documented Homebrew OpenSSL flags; AWS/remote-service tests were not run.

Please consider this report under the published bug-bounty program if eligible. I understand that classification and any award are your decision, and that awards below $100 are account credits rather than cash. No award is assumed.

**AI disclosure and follow-up:** This report, investigation and proposed patch were prepared by OpenAI ChatGPT/Codex (LLMs), with the authorization of the `avs-io` account owner. This is not intended as a one-off report: questions and requested revisions can be addressed through this GitHub account. No live customer data, external service testing or payment credentials were used.

leads.title: Launch HN: Agent37 (YC F26) – Low-cost agent sandboxes for running agents
leads.description: Hey HN, I’m Vishnu from Agent37 ( https://agent37.com ). We build sandboxes for running AI agents at under 10% of the cost of most sandbox providers. Our customers spend an average of $0.37/month per sandbox. You can view a video walkthrough of the product here: https://youtu.be/DK5ISR2tbNo We started as one of those OpenClaw wrapper companies back in February (yup.. judge me). In time we added more and more harnesses. One of the goals I had at the time was to offer a free plan to users, so as to gain more market share. But it was too cost prohibitive to do it right away. Especially since we were bootstrapped and servers were running on my savings. Today we’re actually able to offer the free plan thanks to the optimizations we’ve made since. Over 90% of the new signups we have are just free plan users and they host their personal Hermes/Openclaw/Claude Code etc on our cloud. Our infrastructure cost for the free sandboxes averages around $0.05 to $0.10 per user per month. Here are some techniques that have worked for lowering cost: * When you look at agent harnesses, they have certain patterns in the way they consume CPU and RAM. They need CPU in bursts when they’re initializing or performing certain tasks, but beyond that, they’re often not peaking. They need more RAM for things like browser and computer-use tasks. Once the task is done, usage often comes back down. This is a key insight in lowering cost, so by efficiently managing the CPU/RAM utilization we could lower the cost. * Secondly, you have to skip the hyperscalers when renting the Hosts. I worked at Amazon before and they have 80-90% margins on VMs. So it was an obvious choice once I looked at the prices to go one layer down to vendors like Hetzner and OVH. This alone was probably one of the biggest cost levers in reducing the cost. * Thirdly, you also want to pick a technology stack that lets you efficiently cache and share resources across the host. We use gVisor for better utilization and fast boot times. It lets us use available host memory across sandboxes without reserving a full VM’s memory for each one. There are tradeoffs: our gVisor sandboxes don’t support workloads like Docker-in-Docker or Android emulators. * And finally the size and shape of the hosts you buy also makes a big difference. RAM is typically the bottleneck when it comes to cost and not the CPU. This is specifically true for agent harness workloads, so when buying servers, we optimize for packing more RAM into a given host. We also host full VM sandboxes for workloads that need them, including running Docker at a slightly higher price, but they are still pretty low cost given the rest of the techniques. Overall, my learning has been that just by focusing on a niche of sandbox usecases, and optimizing for it you can give a much better cost/performance tradeoff. I was previously a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and an Engineering Manager at Quantcast. I built Amazon's internal AI chatbot, Diya, and their internal coding harness, Ziya. If you’re someone who’s looking to run agents on sandbox and are exploring a sandbox vendor, come check us out. We’re particularly looking for developers building messaging agents to try their workloads and challenge the limits and economics of our platform. Thanks! https://agent37.com

leads.title: Show HN: PatchWave - Add static analysis and automerge to Dependabot
leads.description: Hey Hacker News, we're Ben, Josh, and Donnie, co-founders of PatchWave. PatchWave is a GitHub App that combines static analysis and eval'ed agents to analyze and (optionally) auto-merge PRs it deems as safe. If a Dependabot PR breaks your CI build, a fix agent works to get CI passing again. Dependabot PRs suck. Nobody likes dealing with them. Most of the time they go ignored or a senior engineer spends their valuable time dealing with them. Before PatchWave, I ran a freelance business charging clients hourly to do exactly this kind of "keep the lights on" work. Even at our small startup, we'd spend Monday mornings dealing with Dependabot PRs. Having a human-in-the-loop working with an agent on these PRs was time consuming and, often, agents would get lazy and not actually validate how an upstream change affected the codebase. And, as the quantity and severity of CVEs increases, merging security updates quickly becomes increasingly important. PatchWave is a set of specialized agents that uses static analysis tools on context we gather deterministically. 1. We pull the changelog, the code diff between versions, security advisories, and CI results. 2. The agent checks out your code in an isolated sandbox, where it uses structural code search, type checkers and your project's own toolchain to understand how your codebase uses each dependency being updated. Every Dependabot PR gets a report. You can see a few examples (against OSS repos) here: https://reports.patchwave.ai/alam00000/bentopdf/pull/913 and https://reports.patchwave.ai/shipshapecode/shepherd/pull/355... 3. If CI fails, we automatically dispatch a fix agent to try to get CI green again. For most PRs, this means updating your code to use a newer API, fixing linting/formatting issues, etc. 4. We have an optional feature that allows auto-merging certain PRs when PatchWave deems them as safe and the PR aligns with your auto-merge policy. Our recommended auto-merge policy is to auto-merge patch/minor/major dev dependencies and patch/minor production dependencies. You can customize this policy or turn auto-merge off entirely. PatchWave will skip auto-merge in a bunch of cases where a human should review. For instance, if provenance changes (e.g., a package that's usually published by GitHub Actions via Trusted Publishing is suddenly published by an API Key), we require human review before merging. Dependabot also instituted an on-by-default 3-day cooldown to reduce the risk of supply chain attacks. If PatchWave makes any changes via a fix agent, we'll always require your review before merge. Currently, PatchWave only works with Dependabot and GitHub. We plan to offer Renovate support in the future. We've eval'ed the agents the most against TypeScript and Ruby, but are always adding to our eval suite to improve accuracy. The fix agent works best with PRs that require modest code changes. For large updates, especially updates that span multiple majors, our fix agent will give up and provide you a remediation plan to help you mitigate. On the privacy/security side of the house, our SOC 2 Type II audit is in progress (see trust.contextbridge.ai). We only run on repos you select, our agents run in a short-lived microVM per run, we use Amazon Bedrock with zero-data-retention, and never train on your code. We're offering 25 free PRs per GitHub org, per month with no credit card required. Additional PRs are billed at about $1/PR, with discounts for higher volume. We also would love to accelerate OSS projects, so reach out to ask about additional free credits. If you hate dealing with Dependabot PRs, we'd love for you to give it a shot and tell us what you think. Josh, Donnie, and I will be around answering any questions and responding to any feedback you have.
